entry.title: More Wheel Sizes?! Cube Is Racing a 30.5-Inch Wheel at Enduro Worlds.
entry.content:
Just when mountain bike wheel sizes seemed to be settling down (basically desensitizing us to the idea of 32″ wheels becoming normal), Cube has something new.

Cube Action Team rider Zakarias Johansen has been spotted in Finale Ligure preparing for the 2026 Enduro World Championships aboard a modified Cube Fritzz with a 30.5-inch front wheel and 29-inch rear. Cube posted it on social media, and eagle-eyed viewers caught on easily.

So, basically a mullet. Except the big wheel is now bigger than a 29er.

The setup appears to be very much in the prototype stage. Johansen is reportedly the only rider at Enduro Worlds using a 30.5-inch front wheel, and Cube isn’t saying much about what they’ve changed on the bike or whether they plan to put the new size into production. Still, lining it up at a World Championship is a pretty big step beyond rolling around a parking lot on a prototype.

Cube Goes 30.5/29

Johansen’s bike is based on the recently released Cube Fritzz, but the normal 29-inch front wheel has been swapped for the new 30.5-inch setup.

From the side, the difference is surprisingly hard to spot. The front wheel is only 1.5 inches larger in diameter than the 29-inch rear, so it doesn’t have the cartoonish look you might expect from some of the 32-inch prototypes we’ve been seeing lately.

The idea also sits somewhere between a normal 29er and the 32-inch wheel experiments popping up across XCO and DH racing. At the Downhill World Championships, Martin Maes went much more extreme with a 32-inch front wheel and a 27.5-inch rear. Johansen’s 30.5/29 setup looks almost conservative by comparison. Kinda.

Why Stop at 30.5 Inches?

The basic argument for a bigger wheel hasn’t changed since 29ers started taking over mountain biking. A larger wheel should carry speed better through rough terrain and roll over holes, rocks, and roots more easily.

But there’s a point where bigger wheels start creating their own problems. Packing them into a short frame gets harder, weight goes up, and forks get complicated. Thirty-two-inch wheels exaggerate all of that.

A 30.5-inch wheel offers a smaller jump from 29 inches, which could make it easier to get some of the rollover benefit without redesigning the entire bike around a huge wheel.

The Fox Podium Apparently Has Room

One of the more interesting details is the fork. Johansen is using the inverted Fox Podium, and it doesn’t appear to have a dedicated 30.5-inch fork.

That’s an important detail. Simply fitting a larger front wheel raises the front of the bike and changes the geometry, so there’s almost certainly more going on than just swapping a different wheel into an otherwise untouched race bike. But we don’t know exactly what magic Cube used to make it work. We’re gonna have to wait and hear more from the riders themselves.

Schwalbe Has the 30.5-Inch Magic Mary

A new wheel size is only useful if someone makes a tire for it. Schwalbe has that part covered.

Johansen’s Cube is running a 30.5-inch Schwalbe Magic Mary up front. The wheel also looks different from Cube’s usual Newmen setup. Newmen already has experience playing with larger wheel sizes, including 32-inch wheels, so another diameter apparently wasn’t out of the question.

Do We Really Need Another Wheel Size?

Maybe not, but people have said the same thing before.

Mountain biking currently has 26, 27.5, 29, 30.5, and 32-inch wheels floating around in one form or another. Add all the possible mullet combinations and the tire wall at your local bike shop could get interesting.

The obvious question is whether 30.5 inches has enough of an advantage over 29 to justify its existence.

That was essentially the question our editor, Zach, asked back in April when rumors of the size first started circulating. At the time, 30.5 looked like it might get buried as the industry pushed toward 32-inch wheels. Now Cube is racing one. But oddly enough, that was for a dropbar bike, not anything near off-road.

Can We Just Call It 750d?

750d uses a 660mm bead seat diameter, sitting between a 29-inch/700c wheel at 622mm and a 32-inch setup at 686mm. WTB previously showed the format on a Moots prototype at MADE, giving us an early look at what an oversized gravel wheel could look like.

At the time, 30.5 inches looked like it could become the new 27.5: a middle step created for riders or bikes where the biggest possible wheel doesn’t quite work. That could make a lot of sense for gravel, but gravel seems to be under the 32″ spell currently.

Keep an eye out, like it or not, 30.5″ (750d) wheels might be coming to a race near you.

entry.title: Brompton C Line Review: A Delightful Way to Get Around, But Choose Your Spec Wisely
entry.content:
Believe it or not, until recently, I had never ridden a folding bike. It’s not that I was actively steering clear of folding bikes; I’ve just never had a reason to ride one – or I didn’t realize I had a reason. But I know they are not only popular, but convenient in many ways. And the Brompton C-Line proved to be exactly that.

The folding bike world is full of passionate riders, just like every other segment of cycling. I mean, the Brompton Mafia is a thing. It’s a group of rabid Brompton users/lovers effortlessly flying all over the world with their bicycles. And it’s pretty rad.

The Sea Otter Classic even holds a Le Mans-style Brompton race every year. It’s really fun, irreverent, and quite the spectacle.

In fact, our Racing Tech Editor, Jordan, competed in the Sea Otter Brompton race this year and podiumed, ’cause that’s what Jordan does… doesn’t matter the bike. Fun times!!

I Got to Take it to MADE

Anywho, the opportunity to ride one arose this year, right before the MADE Show. I usually attend only two bike industry shows a year: the Sea Otter Classic and the MADE Show. I usually drive to both of these shows. Sea Otter is in Monterey, California, and only a 5-6-hour drive for me. And MADE is in Portland, Oregon, and is usually a 2-day drive for me… 3 days if I don’t want to kill myself.

But for this year’s MADE Show, I decided I wanted to fly up to Portland. Zach, my Editor-in-Chief, and I booked our hotel for the show, and it ended up being very close to the venue.

Getting in the rental car to make the short drive to the venue seemed wasteful and silly. And walking sucks, most of the time. So, Zach decided to bring his Tern BYB folder to ride to and from the show, and suggested I try to find a way to do something similar.

I wanted to bring my Wilde Rambler SL, but I didn’t have a proper travel case for it. And a bike that is made to easily handle navigating a crowded airport and flying with it sounded much easier. Plus, I wanted to try a folding bike, period. So, Zach suggested reaching out to Brompton, as we’ve never reviewed one of their bikes on the site before.

So I did.

Folding and Flying with the Brompton

I received the 16″ wheeled Brompton C Line 4-speed a few days before leaving for Portland. I also received the B&W Fold On Case. This hard-shell, suitcase-type case is the perfect size to check at the airport. And the bike fits effortlessly in that case.

The case is not cheap at $269.99 on the Brompton site. If that’s out of your budget, I will say there are a bunch of Brompton riders who will bring their Bromptons folded, out of a case, onto the plane as “carry-ons”. They just stow them in the airplane’s overhead compartment (though you should definitely confirm the airline allows this before trying it).

I opted for the hard case, just for convenience. I packed the C Line into the case, paid the regular “checked bag” price, and away we went. Zero issues. Not one.

Recovering it from baggage claim was just as easy. The case rolled well through the airport and was easy to wield and maneuver through the crowds – though one major difference between the Brompton case and the Tern is that it has two wheels instead of four. The Tern case was easier to wheel through the airport, but the Brompton case will likely be more durable. The handle also extends to a good length and is easy to manipulate up or down.

The Brompton C-Line weighs a claimed 26.1lbs. When packed in the case, it pushed the weight to a little under 44lbs.

When folded, I found the included rolling rack a game changer. It made it a breeze to roll the folded and partially folded C-Line around. The rack also functions as a kickstand, it folds up to rest almost as quickly as you could kick a kickstand.

Riding the Brompton C-Line 4-Speed

Overall, I enjoyed riding the C-Line 4-Speed. I will admit that there was a smidgen of a learning curve riding on 16″ wheels. I think I would’ve preferred riding a bike with 20″ wheels, like Zach’s Tern.

But after a very short time, I got used to its quick, albeit slightly twitchy, handling. The bike is long, so that’s where, as a rider, you find your stability. I will say that I did not care for the tall gearing.

Any hills? Get the 12 Speed Version

There are two drivetrain options for the C Line, a 4-speed and 12-speed. Both versions use the same 11-18t four-speed cassette, but the 12-speed drivetrain adds an internally geared hub with three speeds. The 12-speed version also gets a smaller 50t chainring vs. the 54t on the 4-speed. Granted, the smaller wheels make a big difference when considering chainring sizes, but the easiest 54x18t combination on the 16″ Brompton is roughly equivalent to a 36x20t on a 700c x 35mm tire. Hardly a climbing gear for casual rides.

That means the 12-speed offers much more range: 402% vs. the C-Line 4-speed’s 163%.

I live in the mountains, and that 4-speed gearing up here is a “no-go” for me. I’ve only ridden it a handful of times while home. It rides nicely, but climbing on it is no bueno. My options for review were limited with a short turn around time, but if I had to do it again, I would definitely choose the 12-speed version.

The only real downside to the 12-speed version is that it’s 0.28lbs (127g) heavier and $200 more. Worth it.

Fit

I’m 6’1″, and the bike felt comfy for me while not feeling cramped at all. Brompton does a stellar job of designing the bike to fit a wide variety of riders. You get your choice of low, mid, or high handlebars when ordering. This bike had the high bars, which kept the front end nice and comfortable even with the seat post extended almost to the max.

The proprietary rear derailleur seemed to work fine. When paired with the shifter, they delivered reliable, snappy shifts.

I liked Brompton’s proprietary clamp system that is used to secure the steering mast and for the mid-frame break.

Brompton C-Line 4-Speed Retail & Detail

Retail: $1,950

  • Weight: From 26.12 lb
  • Main frame: Precision-drawn, heat-treated steel tubing with hand brazing and selected auto-brazed joints
  • Rear frame: Hand brazed cold-formed micro-alloy steel tubing
  • Folded size: 25.3″ H x 23” W x 10.6” D
  • Fork: One-piece carbon fork and steerer with magnetic pedal holder
  • Pedals: Brompton folding left-hand and non-folding right-hand pedals
  • Bottom bracket: Square taper
  • Derailleur: Brompton Chain pusher
  • Tires: 16 x 35C Schwalbe Marathon Racer. A puncture-resistant tire with a reflective sidewall
  • Speed: 4-speed
  • Chainset: 6061 forged aluminium crank with 54T chainring and integrated chainguard
  • Rear cassette: 11-13-15-18 teeth
  • Headset: Brompton headset
  • Brakes: Brompton Dual Pivot Calipers
  • Rear Wheel: Double-wall rim, 28 spoke, Brompton Wide ratio 2-speed internal gear hub
  • Front Wheel: Double-wall rim, 28 spokes laced to a Brompton front hub
  • Fenders: Included
  • Rear Rack: Included

Riding in Portland

All in all, I found the Brompton C-Line a pleasure to bring along for the show. It rides well and packs down to an incredibly small and manageable package. And that is really the point here, right?

I mean, sure, the bike rides fine, but man, does it fold down small. Perfect for flying, storing in small spaces, and bringing it along in a small car without the need for an elaborate and expensive bike rack. It’ll just sit in a small truck, the backseat, or that spot on the floor between the front and back seat.

The only bummer, and it’s a small one, is how much of the Brompton uses proprietary parts. Not all of the parts, but some pretty important parts. I get it; they have one of the smallest folding bikes on the market when folded, so some parts are going to need to be specialty/proprietary parts.

And Brompton has a robust support system in place, so replacing and working on their proprietary parts when they break is not that big of a deal. But still, it would be great if you could use the parts that you really wanted when upgrading or repairing stuff.

In Conclusion

I would absolutely recommend this bike to anyone looking for an amazing folding bike that folds down in less than 20 seconds. It’s easy AF to fly with, and a great, fun way to get around at your destination if you decide to fly with it.

I can’t keep the bike, and I am a little sad that I have to return it. I could really use a folding bike in my life. You know, something super easy to throw in a case and fly with, or toss it in the back of my Jeep to just bring along. No racks and locks needed; it’ll easily fit in the back.

Well, as it turns out, after attending the MADE Show, I’ve worked something out for another folding bike review/story, so stay tuned here for that tomfoolery.

It’s going to be pretty awesome. In the meantime, do yourself a favor and hit the link below to check out the Brompton folding bike world.

US.Brompton.com

entry.title: First Rides on Avona Callis 32: 1st Production 32″ Gravel Bike Proves To Be Fast & Agile
entry.content:
Just a couple of weeks ago, we got a sneak peek at this all-new Avona Callis 32″ gravel race bike at Sea Otter Europe, where it was ridden to a UCI World Series race win. About the same time, I was also able to throw a leg over a stock, consumer-friendly spec, then head out of Girona’s city center for a couple of quick rides over two days. And now, it is available to buy, making this the first proper production carbon gravel bike to market on 32″ wheels.

Let’s break down the details. What’s new, how it rides, and how you can get your own 32″ carbon gravel race bike now…

Avona Callis 32 is the first 32″ gravel race bike you can buy

We all knew 32″ gravel bikes were coming. They’ve been popping up all year, winning pro gravel races. Then, back in Girona, Avona made it clear that the big Callis 32 gravel bike would go on sale on October 15th. So, now we have the full details.

From a starting point, the Avona Callis 32 follows the same ethos of the original Callis they debuted just last year. Avona aims to develop high-performance bikes for everyday riders. And even though this bike was ridden to a pro-level gravel win, it was created for all gravel riders looking to go fast.

Now, much of the tech in the new bike is the same as the 700c/29″ wheeled Callis gravel bike that I rode last year. But Avona didn’t simply scale it up and slap bigger wheels on the Callis 32. Instead, they describe their bike development process more as being ‘holistic’. In fact, they too were a bit skeptical of the jump to 32″ at first, so it was digging into all of the data that convinced them to push on.

Holistic bike development was ideally suited for the shift to 32″ wheels

To Avona, holistic design means, instead of just making a bike to be aerodynamic or lightweight or to fit bigger tires & wheels, they strive to look at all performance characteristics and even component specs together.

Aero gains are great, until the point they make a bike too stiff to ride for several hours. Light bikes are nice for big mountain days, but have less of an impact if your climbing is limited. And wider tires and bigger diameter wheels can boost comfort, control, and even lower rolling resistance, as long as they don’t become heavy, sluggish, or unintentionally introduce extra drag.

When considering the jump to 32″ wheels for gravel, Avona first pooled available data, and realized 32″ rolling resistance gains would probably outweigh any aerodynamic losses. So once they had a design and could prototype, they built up identical 700c & 32″ bikes and ran a Virtual Elevation Method rolling resistance simulation on a real-world, out-and-back section of rough gravel track to determine how much energy the bigger wheels could save by smoothing those bumps out. Their findings showed that switching to the bigger wheels saves 11.7W in rolling resistance at 35kph. Then, in the wind tunnel, the aero drag would only add an extra 1-3W penalty.

(Avona share a Whitepaper of their data analysis for those that like to nerd out on the numbers. Plus, there’s also a deep look at Avona’s 32″ pros & cons that led to the development of the Callis 32 in the first place.)

OK, so what all is new?

Back in Girona, I was able to suss out pretty much all the technical similarities with its smaller 700c sibling.

But really, a lot of what makes this new 32″ gravel bike work is Avona’s attention to refining agile big-wheel geometry. They worked hard on refining the big bike’s geometry – and making sure to develop light & responsive 32″ wheels for it – to be sure to create a proper gravel race bike without compromise on the bigger wheels.

Let’s talk 32″ gravel race-tuned geometry

So, contrary to the recent trend of making gravel bikes slacker to go faster off road, the Callis 32 has decidedly steep angles – a 70° headtube and 74° effective seattube angle. Of course to fit that big wheel in front of you with acceptable toe overlap, frame reach is a bit longer, although the 398mm of my size Large test bike wasn’t extreme. Then, it was a relatively long 60mm fork offset that kept fork Trail in check.

And Avona still managed to keep chainstay length surprisingly short at just 440mm thanks to a dramatically curved seattube, super thin chainstays, and 1x only compatibility.

Avona admits that they couldn’t really build a 32″ gravel bike smaller than a size Medium frame without compromising handling, so they didn’t. The Callis 32 comes in just three sizes: M-XL. But since they started with a 30mm offset seatpost and conventional stem lengths, there is still quite a bit of room for adjustment to fit smaller riders. I saw a rider less than 165cm tall test the size M with a 0mm offset post and a slammed 75mm stem, and both her and I were surprised with how well it fit, and how well the bike handled.

It clear that getting bigger riders on 32″ bikes is always going to make the most sense. But Avona’s sharp handling and tight clearances approach proves smaller riders have a chance, too.

Tech details

Beyond the big wheels and properly tuned geometry, the Avona includes a lot of other lightweight gravel race bike technologies.

  • lightweight carbon frame
  • internal frame storage & mounts to fit 2 full-size water bottles
  • 55mm max tire, with 6mm clearance (not enough for the 2.4″ Aspens on adventure focused 32″ bikes, but yes to the 2.15″ Aspen ST)
  • 1x and electronic shift only; max 50T chainring
  • Boost chainline, Boost rear axle spacing (12x148mm) & Road Boost front (12x110mm)
  • UDH
  • threaded BSA bottom bracket
  • proprietary D-shaped aero seatpost with hidden wedge-style clamp
  • fully integrated cable routing through the ‘sealed’ headset
  • FM160 flat mount rear brake (160 or 180mm rotors)
  • 898g claimed frame weight (size M painted, but without any hardware like the storage door, seatpost clamp, axle, or hanger)
  • 409g claimed fork weight, painted & uncut

OK, so how does it ride?

Fit & First Impressions

At 185cm tall (+/-6’1″), it’s not really a stretch to fit me on bigger wheels (like on the 750D Jumbo). Avona has me on a Large with a middle-of-the-road fit – stem & seatpost wise. But still, about half of the 32″ bikes I have ridden so far (~75% being mountain bikes) could be described as muted, if not specifically sluggish – even if ride data suggests most were actually quicker than comparable 29ers. So, I was cautiously optimistic to try out my first carbon 32″ bike, and the first real production 32″ gravel bike.

Even though I’m quite tall, I most often size down to a Medium on dropbar bikes. But even with that in mind, I didn’t feel stretched out on the Large Callis 32. The 398mm Reach isn’t much more than most L gravel bikes these days, and the 598mm Stack is actually lower than almost all other gravel bikes I’ve ridden this year. Chainstay length is even the same as a fast-feeling 700c gravel bike I’ve been riding lately, just 10-15mm longer than most other 700c gravel bikes I’ve been testing lately.

Out on gravel road & trail?

I had the chance to put in two different rides on the new 32″ Callis during my limited time with it. First, was a pretty chill late afternoon ride, mixing city tarmac and fast, smooth gravel roads. The second, a morning ride on a mix of gravel – Champagne hardpack, some choppy car-induced brake bumps & soft deep gravel outside of the center of Girona, plus a bit of bumpy singletrack along the river resulting from the remnants of muddy MTB ruts.

My immediate feeling on the road then hardpack was how effortlessly the bike was to ride quickly. I cruised along the streets, drafting roadies with seemingly no effort – even rolling on 50mm gravel tires. In the dirt, the wheels spun up quickly when I stomped on the pedals. And it required seemingly little effort to maintain speed.

When riding gravel roads, I didn’t feel like it required any additional effort to change directions. But when I ended up on twisty singletrack, it did feel like I probably had to work a little harder through the turns. That feeling was a bit more exaggerated on tight ups and downs that robbed my momentum, where I could feel it took more effort to re-accelerate and tuck through low-speed turns at the same time.

But notably, I barely felt the brake bumps and just rolled over dried-out ruts & ridges. Maintaining speed on smooth tracks was nice. But the slightly rougher ones were where it felt like the bigger wheels and lower tire pressure (~5psi less than usual) really shone. And I think credit is due here for the Faserwerk wheels too, which thankfully didn’t feel overly stiff (an issue I personally notice with many deeper aero gravel race wheels).

Why does it feel so quick, even with bigger wheels?

Avona’s 32″ frame at a claimed 898g (M, painted) is actually lighter than their 700c version, offsetting about +100-200g extra weight in the wheels, so their complete Callis 700 & Callis 32 bikes are effectively the same total weight. So the whole 32″ bike is as light as many 700c bikes.

Plus, I’ve ridden 32″ XC bikes with >2500g wheelsets with 1700g of additional tire weight. Avona’s own Faserwerk Kornkreis 32″ wheels on DT 350 hubs like I rode are said to weigh just 1567g, making them no heavier really than many aero 700c gravel wheelsets. And the 50mm Schwalbe tires add about 1300g on top of that, maybe 100g more than a 700c setup.

Really, it all adds up – light overall bike weight, especially light wheels, light and not too wide tires, reduced Trail, steep head angle, and a forward-leaning rider weight balance.

To me the Avona Callis 32 simply felt quick, not really possessing any of the sluggishness I had felt when riding more adventure- or XC-focused 32″ bikes on gravel roads. Several pro cyclists I have discussed 32″ wheels with told me that the bigger-wheeled bikes felt slower, but measured faster lap times without fail. As someone not racing, that doesn’t really sound appealing to me.

But riding the Callis 32, which actually feels faster to my amateur rider brain, now I’m coming around to the idea that 32″ wheels could appeal to the average gravel bike rider, too. Not just the gravel racer.

Looks like I’m going to need to spend a lot more time riding 32″ bikes to keep building a larger baseline of comparison. In the meantime, this new carbon Callis 32 gravel bike seems like a solid starting point for production 32″ gravel bikes.

Avona Callis 32″ gravel bike – Pricing, options & availability

The new Avona Callis 32 is actually available now, making it the first production carbon gravel bike you can buy on 32″ wheels as far as I know. Three complete bike specs are available, in three paint colors – clear over carbon, Deep Olive green, Ultra Violet purple, or primed ready-to-paint.

As well as a ‘rolling chassis’ frame kit that includes frame, fork, headset, seatpost, 1-piece integrated cockpit, and a set of 32″ wheels starting at 4800€ for you to build up with the drivetrain of your choice.

Complete builds start at 5800€ with SRAM Rival AXS Xplr or 6600€ for Force. The SRAM Red AXS Xplr build starts at 9000€ including a power meter. (A GRX 1x Di2 build will come in 2027, as well.) All feature the 45mm deep Faserwerk Kornkreis wheels on DT 240 hubs standard. But can be upgraded to stiffer 62mm deep Newmen wheels with steel (+120€) or carbon (+470€) spokes for a bit more. All Avona builds are semi-custom, letting you choose post offset, bar width, stem & crank length, chainring size, cassette spread, and tires to get your perfectly dialed setup. Plus, all include CeramicSpeed UFO waxed chains out of the box,

Order your now to either pick it up from an Avona dealer bikeshop, or to have it shipped directly to you throughout Europe, the US, and South Africa.

Avona.cc

entry.title: Allied FITZ Review: A Lighter, and Very Fun, Take on the Modern Trail Bike
entry.content:
Allied Cycle Works launched the FITZ back in February. Along with the XC-oriented BC 40, the FITZ is only Allied’s second mountain bike model and its first entry in the broad trail bike market. With a lightweight carbon frame, 140mm of travel front and rear, and a surprisingly progressive geometry, the FITZ landed squarely in that Goldilocks do-it-all category — on paper anyway. And with a stated goal of bringing lightweight back to the trail bike category, it certainly appeared that Allied was offering something a little different.

With the weight of many trail bikes inflating above the 30-pound mark in recent years, it was that last part that really appealed to me. And since the FITZ came out last winter, I’ve been eager to throw a leg over one. It took a few months to arrange a test bike, but I’ve been testing the FITZ for the past 6 weeks or so. Rather than the typical 140/140mm setup, I opted for the 150mm version, which I thought would be a better fit for my terrain and riding style. 

Allied FITZ Details

We covered the FITZ when it launched back in February, and you can check out all the details here. Long story short, it’s got a carbon frame with 140mm of rear travel that’s typically meant to be paired with a 140mm fork. It’s compatible with 150mm forks, and the rear travel can also be bumped to 150mm with a longer-stroke shock. 

It rolls on 29-inch wheels front and rear and has most of the features common on modern mountain bikes, including internal cable routing, molded rubber frame protection, and in-frame storage. At the same time, the brand focused on keeping the weight as low as possible, which the designers say is one of the reasons why it went with a fairly straightforward 4-bar Horst-Link suspension layout. 

According to Allied, complete bike weights start at 26 lbs for the top-tier XX SL build, which is very light for a 140mm travel trail bike. That’s only 2 pounds heavier than many of the latest XC race bikes, with 20mm more travel at both ends. Weights increase incrementally from there, but the starting point is quite low for a trail bike. 

Geometry-wise, Allied didn’t tip-toe into the trail bike category. Instead, they jumped right in and gave the FITZ what I consider to be a very modern do-it-all geometry. Reach numbers are in the typical range with 480mm on a size large, and the seat tube angle is adequately steep at 76.6°. The 64.5° head angle (with 140mm fork) seals the deal and really speaks to this bike’s ride-anything intentions.  

My Test Bike

The FITZ is sold as a frame kit, or in three complete builds: SRAM XX SL, SRAM XO, and SRAM GX. When purchasing, buyers have numerous customization options, including the frame and logo color, fork, shock, handlebar, seatpost, wheels, and more. Opting for a custom color or making any changes to the stock component spec may change the final price, depending on what you choose.  

As mentioned, I opted for the 150mm setup, which is one of many options when purchasing the FITZ. All of the stock builds come with 140mm travel Fox 36 SL forks. Since the 36 SL tops at 140mm, the bump to 150mm moves you onto a non-SL Fox 36 Factory with the Grip X2 damper (+$25). Similarly, the stock builds come with 210x50mm Fox Float shocks providing 140mm of rear wheel travel. Buyers have the option to upgrade to a 210x55mm Fox Float X (+$25), and the longer stroke increases rear wheel travel to 150mm. 

Given that the Float X has a longer stroke, but the same eye-to-eye measurement, the increase to 150mm of rear travel doesn’t impact the FITZ’s geometry. The addition of 10mm of fork travel, however, relaxes the head tube angle and seat tube angles by roughly half a degree, putting them right around 64° and 76°, respectively. 

I ended up with the XO build, which, other than the suspension, is mostly stock with an XO AXS drivetrain, We Are One Whisp Wheels with Industry Nine 1/1 hubs, and a OneUp cockpit. Interestingly, my test bike arrived with a matching set of Vittoria’s beefy Mazza tires front and rear. I’ve been a fan of the Mazza for years, so I wasn’t disappointed, but the faster-rolling Vittoria Aggaro or Maxxis Rekon are the only options when buying. It also came with Shimano XT 4-piston brakes with 203mm front / 180mm rear Ice Tech rotors, which doesn’t appear to be one of the customization options either.

On my scale, the FITZ weighed in at 29.8 pounds. While that’s a bit heavier than the starting weight of 26 pounds, I think that’s still pretty light for a 150/150mm travel bike with meaty tires. The stock build with the 140mm 36 SL fork and lower-profile tires would surely save some weight. As tested, the FITZ with the SRAM XO build and 150/150mm upgrade retails for $8,815.

Riding the Allied FITZ

The FITZ makes a good first impression, and I think it’s a really nice-looking bike. Sure, the tiny hump in the top tube takes a little getting used to, but I stopped noticing it pretty quickly. Otherwise, I generally dig the tube shapes, reinforced head tube, and somewhat minimalist design of the frame. I also appreciate that the bottom of the downtube slopes to the bottom bracket, providing a bit more frame clearance than many bikes which stick out a bit more these days.

After making a few fit adjustments and dialing in suspension pressures, I took to the trails. In the past six weeks, I’ve been riding the FITZ off and on, switching between the Gen 6 Santa Cruz Tallboy and the new Yeti MT. I’ve been riding it out the door to my local trails in Reno, NV, and venturing up to the Tahoe/Truckee area for a bit of terrain variety. It’s seen a mix of everything, including fast-paced XC-style riding, some janky hand-built skidders, and some long climbs and sustained descents. It hasn’t rained in a while, so it has been pretty dusty and loose, too. 

Climbing

I felt comfortable immediately on the FITZ. The reach, seat tube angle, and cockpit setup put me in a neutral seated pedaling position that worked well for me on mellower terrain and steep climbs alike. At no point did the seat tube angle feel too steep with too much weight on my hands, nor too slack with a wandering front end. I’m a big fan of OneUp’s Carbon bars for their comfortable ride feel, and there were plenty of stack spacers to adjust bar height if needed. 

On the climbs and through the flats, the FITZ did what I wanted and responded to handling inputs well. It’s not super snappy or hyperresponsive like an XC race bike, nor is it bulky and lethargic the way some enduro bikes can feel. Instead, it lands nicely in the middle, and I think it handles exactly how a trail bike should. There are more agile trail bikes, the new Tallboy, for example, but I had no issues climbing up techy sections or negotiating tight terrain or switchbacks, even with the 150mm fork and slightly slacker head tube angle.

For its travel bracket, the FITZ undoubtedly has a light and lively character, and that contributes to its energetic pedaling feel. It has a quick demeanor and eagerness to keep the pace up, especially compared to the heavier Yeti MT, for example. I’m not saying the Yeti doesn’t pedal or climb well, just that the FITZ has a bit more pep with an efficient pedaling platform and 3 pounds less junk in the trunk. And that’s with the slower-rolling Vittoria Mazza rear tire.

I set up the rear suspension a touch on the stiff side, as close to 25% sag as I could get, for pedaling support — and bigger hits — and that sacrificed a little small bump compliance. Still, I had no shortage of climbing traction, but I’m sure the grippy and aggressive Mazza rear tire contributed to that a bit. And while I appreciated that traction, I’d still be inclined to swap that rear tire out for something faster, like the Vittoria Aggaro or Kenda Ripper Trail for a bit less rolling resistance.

Descending

I didn’t really know what to expect from a trail bike that had low weight as one of its design priorities, but I quickly learned the FITZ was a blast on the descents. Again, it felt lively and agile for a 150/150mm bike, but certainly did not lack confidence or capability in steeper or rougher terrain. I’m sure some of that is due to the 150mm setup and beefier tires, but the geometry undoubtedly plays an outsized role in its versatility.

With a 480mm reach, 210mm dropper (size large), and comfortable cockpit setup, I felt right at home on mellower terrain, machine-built flow trails, or rolling into steeper slabs and technical rock gardens. The 440mm rear center length is the same on all sizes, and I thought it felt perfect on the size large. I can’t speak to the other sizes, but it felt nicely balanced front and rear, plenty stable at higher speeds, yet far from a monster truck. Importantly, it was easy for me to find and stay in the sweet spot and keep the front end weighted for traction. This bike absolutely railed through berms. 

The aforementioned light, lively character carried over to the descents, too. It was easy to get the front or both wheels off the ground, work the terrain, and pop all the side hits. At the same time, it didn’t flinch when jumping straight into blown-out skidders and steep rock rolls. Sure, the 150mm fork and 64-ish-degree head angle helped, but I seriously didn’t think twice about taking it down the toughest trails I typically ride. That’s got plenty to do with the burlier build, but the FITZ’s geometry makes it a bike I’d ride anywhere.

While some might question the run-of-the-mill 4-bar suspension layout, modern shocks are fantastic, and I liked the way it rode. It was easy to set up, and while it might not have been the most sensitive off the top, it delivered in every other way. The mid-stroke was supportive to push off of, yet nice and active when smoothing over chunk and chatter. It responded to big hits with composure, didn’t wallow, and I never once bottomed it out, even when getting full travel. So, even if it doesn’t make headlines, it rides well and helps keep the FITZ’s weight down.

Allied also managed to make the FITZ very quiet. I didn’t notice any chain slap noises, and the internally routed brake line and dropper cable never made a sound. It was so quiet that I started noticing the front brake hose barely tapping the handlebar. The magnetic hatch on the in-frame storage compartment was also silent, yet very easy to remove and replace. The opening of the compartment isn’t the biggest and the included storage bag is fairly long and narrow, but it’s certainly useful for stashing some tools, even if it won’t fit a burrito. 

Spec Report

The XO build is honestly fantastic, and my complaints are few. The Fox suspension worked flawlessly, as did the SRAM XO drivetrain. This was my first time riding the We Are One Whisp wheels, and at ~1,500 grams for the set, they’re probably one of the contributors to the FITZ’s light, energetic ride feel. I thought the ride quality was pleasantly neutral, and I appreciated the quick pickup of the Industry Nine 1:1 hubs.

I’m a big fan of Shimano brakes, and the new XT’s work really well. No, they aren’t as powerful as Mavens, but not every bike needs DH brakes either. They’ve got ample power, excellent modulation, and in my experience, they never make any noise. The OneUp stem, handlebar, and grips make for a great cockpit setup, and I wouldn’t change a thing. Likewise, the OneUp V3 dropper just plain works and is easy to service if needed.

On top of that dropper, however, the Fizik Aidon X5 reconfirmed that I just don’t get along with Fizik saddles. I found it to be stiff, and the edges of the pressure-relief cutout were very noticeable and uncomfortable. Saddle choice is personal, obviously, but I’d swap it out immediately if I were keeping this bike. As mentioned above, I’d probably keep the Mazza tire up front, but would switch to something a little faster-rolling in the back for the majority of my riding. Not that the Mazza tires are an option when purchasing anyway.

My Takeaway

If you couldn’t already tell, I really enjoyed riding the Allied FITZ. To me, it’s exactly what a trail bike should be, and that’s a single bike to do it all. If this was the only bike I had in my garage, it would have me covered for pretty much any ride outside of the XC race course. It’s lighter than most of its direct competitors, and it pedals and climbs efficiently and comfortably, making it a solid choice for big vert and/or big mileage. It handles well and is a blast to ride whether you’re ripping the after-work XC loop or doing laps on more aggressive terrain — especially in the 150mm configuration I tested.

Unfortunately, I didn’t get to try the 140/140mm setup, but based on my experience I’m inclined to believe it’s a heck of a lot of fun, too. It strikes me as a great option for people who want a lighter bike for long rides and want/need more travel than XC or downcountry rigs offer. For the folks lamenting that trail bikes have gotten heavier over the years, the FITZ might be just what you’re looking for. I think it’s a very impressive first effort from Allied, and I’m intrigued to see what they cook up next.  

alliedcycleworks.com

entry.title: Ornot Introduces the Fog Eater Hooded Rain Jacket so You Can Stay Dry, Ornot
entry.content:
Ornot made a name for itself with its high-quality, technical, minimally-branded cycling apparel that doesn’t make you look like a rolling billboard. The latest addition to the lineup is the brand-new Fog Eater Hooded Rain Jacket, a fitting name, considering Ornot is based in often-foggy San Francisco, California. It’s made with a 3L Pertex Shield fabric, boasts 20k/20k waterproof/breathability, and packs into its own pocket when not in use. Let’s take a look.

Ornot Fog Eater Hooded Rain Jacket Details

Ornot tells us that the Fog Eater was inspired by a mountaineering shell and adapted for the bike. First and foremost, it’s a rain jacket, and it’s made with a 3-layer Pertex Shield fabric with fully taped seams and a PFC-free DWR to give it a 20k waterproof / 20k breathability rating. At just 87gsm, this fabric also helps keep it lightweight, and the jacket weighs a claimed 280 grams in size medium. 

Ornot says the Fog Eater has a slim but slightly relaxed fit designed to layer underneath and still perform on the bike, but is relaxed enough to not look out of place with a pair of pants. The cycling-oriented fit includes a shorter cut in the front, a dropped tail for extra coverage in the back, and articulated arms for comfort in the riding position. It’s got a drawcord hem and a three-way adjustable hood that’s designed to fit under a helmet when you need to seal out the elements.

The Fog Eater has a 2-way front zipper to vent from the top or bottom or access your jersey pockets. It also features internal drop pockets, a zippered rear pocket, plus two zippered hand warmer pockets. The left hand pocket doubles as a stuff sack, and the jacket packs down to a 6” x 6” pouch when you aren’t wearing it. And like any good cycling apparel, the Fog Eater has reflective details to make you visible when you’re cutting through the fog.

Specs and Features

  • 87 gsm 3-layer Pertex Shield, 20K waterproof / 20K breathable 
  • Fully taped seams, PFC-free DWR
  • 280 grams (size medium) 
  • Packs into its own pocket
  • 3-point adjustable hood w/ rain peak, fits under helmet
  • Adjustable hem
  • Hand warmer pockets (left pocket is a stuff sack)
  • Internal drop pockets, zippered rear pocket
  • Reflective details
  • Sizes:
    • Men’s XS – XXL
    • Women’s: XS – XL
  • Colors:
    • Men’s: Stone Green / Citron
    • Women’s: Citron

Pricing and Availability

The Fog Eater Hooded Rain Jacket retails for $325 and is available now direct from Ornot. Head to the Ornot website to learn more, or check out their full line of cycling and lifestyle apparel, most of which is made in the USA.

ornotbike.com

entry.title: Silca Ressurects Omata: the Iconic Analog Cycling Computer
entry.content:
Silca just announced it acquired and resurrected Omata, the world’s first analog cycling computer with internal GPS. After the announcement, Silca will release a limited run of the iconic Omata ($800) devices, made in-house at its Indianapolis facility…

Silca Omata Quick Hits

  • Made in-house at Silca
  • $800
  • Distraction-Free Analog Dial: Clean mechanical interface displaying speed, distance, ascent, and ride time.
  • Digital in the Background: GPS internal computer records standard FIT files for training logs and data transfer.
  • Improved Weather Resistance: Triple-barrier lip seal around bezel and Gore-Tex membrane over the barometric pressure sensor.
  • Seamless Syncing: Quick .fit file uploads via the Omata Utility App for iOS or via a USB-C connection.
  • Smart Tracking: Features Auto-Pause and GPS-Fix to seamlessly track your route without manual intervention.
  • Omata is iOS-compatible only.
  • New Mounting System: Omata works with existing Garmin or Wahoo mounts.

Omata Refresh

Longtime readers of The Radavist will remember when Omata first launched back in 2016. At the time, it was the world’s first mechatronic cycling computer (a digital unit with analog movement), and it presents a refined yet restrained design without sacrificing the performance expected of a modern digital device. Built as an intentional alternative to screen-fatiguing, noisy digital electronics, Omata captures data silently in the background while displaying real-time metrics through a mechanical dial.

Made by Silca

Encased in an aluminum housing, Omata features an intuitive rotating bezel for switching modes, USB-C charging, improved weather resistance, and integrated ANT+ connectivity. With its latest firmware update, available to Apple iOS users, Omata can seamlessly pair with external sensors to record ride analytics such as power and heart rate, keeping the interface distraction-free while capturing essential information in the background.

Silca redesigned Omata’s internal circuit board, battery system, and outer housing around the legacy analog “movements” to modernize the hardware. Production and final assembly were moved to the brand’s Indianapolis facility, making it one of the only cycling computers assembled in the United States. The Silca team also redesigned the instrument’s weather sealing, integrating a custom triple-barrier lip seal for the rotating bezel and a Gore-Tex membrane over the barometric pressure sensor for improved moisture resistance, while also adding a versatile square mounting cleat compatible with standard Garmin or Wahoo mounts, allowing riders to swap between computers and bikes easily.

Release and Production

Because Silca’s production run is limited and production is not quick, Silca will be releasing Omata in small batches until sold out. This limited production model does make these units only available in the US. Please reach to Silca out if you are international and interested in a unit.

See more at Silca.

The post Silca Ressurects Omata: the Iconic Analog Cycling Computer appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Omata Classic Analog Cycling Computer is Back, Updated and Now Built by Silca!
entry.content:
The mechanical watch-inspired Omata cycling computer is back in limited numbers, thanks to its acquisition by Silca. Unique for its traditional analog watch-style display, backed by high-tech GPS and connected sensor tracking inside, the Omata cycling computer is probably the classiest way to track your ride – and one of the more expensive. It also happens to probably be the only way to stay on top of your ride metrics without staring at a screen.

It’s totally niche. So, it completely makes sense that Silca would be the one to snap it up to re-issue it to discerning cyclists.

Omata by Silca: analog cycling computer to reduce screentime

It’s been a decade since we first saw the Omata – already expensive back then as a Kickstarter campaign. And this is definitely still a niche cycling computer. Pretty much every other GPS and ride tracking computer has gone the way of bigger, more vivid displays, touchscreens, haptic buttons, voice control, and even solar power top-ups.

But Silca acquired Omata not to change it, but to ensure cyclists can still buy a modern, connected ride tracker, without having a big computer screen strapped to the front of their bike.

“At Silca, we are obsessed with the intersection of beauty, precision, and performance. Omata [One] is a masterpiece of functional art. We acquired Omata because we believed it was a product that should continue to exist in this world. Sadly, it relies on a finite supply of legacy Seiko components; so, each unit carries the weight of rarity. By bringing hand-assembly to our Indianapolis facility, we are ensuring each of these stunning instruments is tested for lasting performance.”

– Josh Poertner, Silca CEO

What’s new since we last caught up with the Omata One?

The biggest shift here is that the new Silca Omata computer is now being assembled at Silca’s US headquarters in Indiana vs. Oulu, Finland for the original device.

There are a few updates since we first covered it, although most of these have been around for a while. The biggest there is that a couple of years after its debut, Omata added compatibility with most modern sensors – like heart rate, cadence, power – via a connected iOS app so you could track more data in the background.

Silca has also apparently redesigned the Omata’s internal circuit board, battery, and outer housing to “modernize the hardware” a bit. One functional improvement is upgraded weatherproofing, using a new triple-barrier lip seal for the device’s rotating outer bezel and the addition of a Gore-Tex membrane over its barometric pressure sensor to keep moisture out. It also means the new device only connects to ANT+ sensors no – no more Bluetooth compatibility.

The housing also now gets a new “versatile square mounting cleat” that makes it compatible with both Garmin & Wahoo interfaces, so you can use the favorite mount you already have on your bike(s). Plus, Silca will let you pick one of their 3D-printed titanium Chisela computer mounts for free when you buy a new Omata.

What stays the same?

Mostly though, Silca hasn’t messed with it.

It’s effectively still the exact same mechatronic cycling computer, i.e. a fully digital GPS device that converts electronic ride tracking data into the mechanical movement of the arms of its analog face. No smartphone notifications or live mapping. Just a simple dial showing current speed, ride distance, accumulated elevation, and ride duration.

Tech details

  • custom analog watch-style display of current ride stats
  • Seiko-precision mechatronic display of electronic ride data
  • ride data exported as .FIT file
  • bespoke Omata Custom Numerals font for clear visibility
  • machined 6063 aluminum housing
  • metric (dark gray) or imperial (white) units of measure
  • 63mm diameter x 17mm thick x 83g
  • multi-channel GPS tracking
  • on-board accelerometer, barometric pressure & temperature sensors
  • ANT+ connectivity only (no BLE sensors)
  • iOS-only (Apple iPhone) connected compatibility
  • 17-hour ride time
  • USB-C rechargeable
  • compatible with Garmin & Wahoo mounts
  • hand-assembled in Indianapolis, IN, USA

Silca Omata cycling computer – Pricing, options & availability

Explaining that only a finite supply of the discontinued ‘legacy’ Japanese mechatronic Seiko movements at the heart of the analog cycling computer exist, Silca says the updated Omata will remain strictly a limited edition. You can still get one of the new US-made computers, though, in either a white imperial units face or a dark gray metric face. But you can only buy it in the United States. Sorry, international Silca shoppers.

The new Silca-made Omata cycling computer sells for $800, which also includes a Silca Chisela 3D-printed titanium mount of your choice, to best fit your bike’s cockpit setup.

Snap yours up today before they disappear!

Silca.cc

entry.title: Moots County Line Splits the Difference Between Road and Gravel With 42mm Tire Clearance
entry.content:
The new Moots County Line is Steamboat Springs’ answer for riders who spend most of their time on pavement but don’t turn around when the road turns to dirt. I know, it’s splitting hairs, and we’ve heard this pitch before, but damn, this bike looks so good that it doesn’t matter. It’s designed around a 38mm tire, clears up to 42mm, uses road gearing, and keeps relatively short 425mm chainstays.

Moots calls it an all-road bike, and the new County Line replaces the Vamoots 33 in the lineup. The standard version uses straight-gauge 3/2.5 titanium tubing, while a lighter double-butted County Line RSL is coming in early 2027.

It’s a Moots Thats Not Quite a Routt, Not Quite a Vamoots

Moots already covers both ends of this range. The Routt has followed modern gravel toward bigger rubber and rougher terrain, and now centers on a 50mm tire. The Vamoots remains a dedicated road bike.

The County Line lands between them.

Moots designed it around the mixed-surface riding near its Steamboat Springs home, but the idea is familiar: a fast bike for pavement and smooth dirt roads. The kinda where you spend plenty of time on pavement before detouring onto fast county-road gravel and eventually returning to asphalt.

For Moots, the goal is to keep the familiar feel and efficiency of a road bike while adding enough tire volume and stability for loose surfaces and rough pavement. Plus, it needs to bring that Moots energy, that classic look with a supreme road feel. This isn’t a gravel bike with slick tires. It’s a road-oriented titanium bike that’s much less picky about what counts as a road.

Designed Around a 38mm Tire

The County Line is designed around a 38c tire, with clearance for up to 42c. 38mm is becoming a popular size, and we’re seeing lots of performance all-road tires pushing up to this limit.

Speaking of which, the bikes come with Vittoria Corsa Pro Control 38c tires, which says a lot about where Moots expects this bike to live. These aren’t chunky gravel tires trying to make a road bike survive off-road. They’re fast, high-volume road tires with enough cushion and grip for hard-packed dirt and broken pavement.

Moots says the larger tire platform adds grip and comfort without bringing along the weight and volume of a full modern gravel setup. That makes the County Line a pretty different proposition from the Routt.

If your rides regularly involve rocky doubletrack and deep gravel, the Routt still makes more sense. If “gravel” means well-maintained dirt roads between stretches of pavement, the County Line is aimed directly at that use.

Road Gearing Stays

Moots didn’t use the extra tire clearance as an excuse to go full gravel with the drivetrain. The County Line uses a 45mm road chainline and supports both 1x and 2x configurations. Maximum chainring size is 50T for 1x or 52/36T for 2x, though Moots’ complete 2x bikes are spec’d with SRAM 48/35T cranksets.

That’s paired with a BSA 68mm threaded bottom bracket, flat-mount brakes, 160mm front and rear rotors, and a UDH derailleur hanger. It fully supports front-derailleur setups, and electronic routing comes standard. Moots does not offer internally routed mechanical shifting.

New Carbon All-Road Fork and Integrated Front End

The County Line gets a new Moots carbon all-road fork with a D-shaped steerer.

Brake hoses run internally through the Moots titanium stem and down through the fork, cleaning up the front end without abandoning the titanium stem that fits the rest of the bike so well. The updated fork measures 382mm axle-to-crown and comes in 45mm and 52mm offsets, depending on frame size.

Moots uses the different offsets to keep steering feel balanced across the eight-size range. The smaller 48, 50, and 52cm bikes use the 52mm offset, while sizes 54 through 62 move to 45mm.

More Stable Than a Road Bike, Without Gravel-Bike Length

The geometry moves slightly toward gravel, but Moots didn’t stretch the County Line into a long, lazy bike. Every size uses 425mm chainstays, short by current gravel standards, which should keep the rear lively.

Head angles range from 70 degrees on the smallest 48cm frame to 72.75 degrees on the 60 and 62cm bikes. Seat angles move the other way, starting at 74.75 degrees on the 48 and gradually settling to 73.5 degrees on the largest sizes.

The idea is more stability and confidence than a traditional road race bike, without the stretched wheelbase and slower handling that often come with a modern gravel chassis.

Straight-Gauge Titanium Standard, RSL Coming in 2027

The standard County Line uses straight-gauge 3/2.5 titanium tubing. Moots describes that as the more forgiving version and expects it to be the right choice for most riders.

Then there’s the County Line RSL. Starting in early 2027, buyers can upgrade the same platform to Moots’ ride-tuned, double-butted RSL tubing. The RSL frame uses less material where it isn’t needed, dropping weight while giving the bike a quicker, more direct feel under power.

Rather than maintaining two separate all-road platforms, Moots is treating RSL as a premium frame upgrade.

Same bike, different tubing.

That should make the decision pretty straightforward: standard County Line for the classic Moots ride, RSL if weight and sharper response matter more. Moots hasn’t published a frame weight for either version yet.

Fenders, Racks, and a Third Bottle

The County Line may lean toward the road side, but Moots didn’t strip away all the practical stuff. Standard frames get fender mounts, optional upper rack mounts, and room for a third bottle underneath the downtube.

The RSL gives some of that up to keep things lighter. Moots lists the standard bike with fender mounts, while the RSL does without them.

Both frames use a standard 27.2mm seatpost, and it supports electronic dropper posts if someone really wants to push the County Line farther into dirt territory.

Moots County Line Complete Builds

Moots is offering four complete builds at launch, split between SRAM Force and Red and between 1x and 2x.

The Force 1x gets SRAM Force XPLR E1 13-speed with a 44T chainring and 10-46T cassette. It rolls on HED Vanquish 45 rims with DT Swiss 350 hubs and Vittoria Corsa Pro Control 38c tires.

Builds include a Zipp SL 80 Race handlebar, Moots titanium stem, Moots Ti Cinch seatpost, Chris King Inset 7 headset, Chris King TF30 bottom bracket, and custom WTB Gravelier Ti saddle.

The Red 1x follows the same basic formula but moves to SRAM Red XPLR and Chris King R45D hubs.

The 2x builds switch to SRAM’s road drivetrains with 48/35T cranksets and 10-36T cassettes.

All four complete bikes use the Moots Carbon Allroad fork, Zipp SL 80 Race handlebar, Moots titanium stem and seatpost, HED Vanquish 45 rims, and 38c Vittoria Corsa Pro Control tires.

Moots County Line Pricing

The standard County Line is available to order starting now, so go get yourself that Halloween present you know you deserve.

  • County Line Frameset: $5,499
  • County Line Force 1x: $9,999
  • County Line Force 2x: $10,599
  • County Line Red 1x: $12,499
  • County Line Red 2x: $12,999

Moots.com

entry.title: Moots County Line All-Road
entry.content:
Moots just announced its County Line all-road bike, filling the space between its 50 mm Routt gravel bike and Vamoots road bike designed around a 38 mm tire…

Moots County Line Quick Hits

  • Frameset: $5,499
  • 1X or 2X Drivetrain Compatibility: A 45mm road chainline supports both 1x and 2x drivetrains, with clearance for up to a 50T 1x or 52/36T 2x setup.
  • Fully Integrated Front End: A new Moots carbon all-road fork uses a D-shaped steerer for internal brake routing through the Moots titanium stem.
  • All-Road Geometry: More stable than a traditional road platform, with size-specific 45mm and 52mm fork offsets to keep handling balanced across the full size range.
  • Built for Long-Day Rides: Fender mounts come standard, with optional upper rack mounts and room for a third bottle under the downtube.

Moots Drop-Bar Family

Gravel bikes have changed quickly. As tires got bigger and terrain got rougher, Moots’ dedicated gravel model, the Routt, moved with them. Today it’s built around a 50 mm tire, with room for considerably more. At the other end of the spectrum, the Vamoots remains what it has always been: a dedicated road bike.

38 mm All-Road Geometry

This new chassis is designed around a 38 mm tire, made for rides that move naturally between pavement and fast, well-maintained dirt roads. More tire, stability, and control than a traditional road bike, without the size, gearing, or off-road emphasis of a modern gravel bike.

County Line is designed to feel quick and responsive on pavement, with more stability and control than a traditional road bike when the surface gets loose. The 38 mm tire platform adds grip and comfort without the weight and volume of a modern gravel setup, while road gearing and relatively short 425 mm chainstays keep the bike efficient and lively under power.

County Line Pricing

  • Frameset $5,499.00
  • Force 1x $9,999.00
  • Force 2x $10,599.00

entry.title: Salsa Updates the Beargrease Fat Bike
entry.content:
Now in its fourth generation, the 27.5-wheeled Beargrease race bike just got a major overhaul from Salsa. This wholly redesigned chassis is longer, lower, and slacker for stable handling in all kinds of winter conditions…

Salsa Beargrease Quick Hits

  • Bare Bones: Beargrease Carbon frameset $1,999
  • Entry Tier: Beargrease Aluminum Eagle 70 complete $1,999
  • Top of the Line: Beargrease Carbon GX AXS complete $5,999
  • Five sizes (XS–XL)
  • Slacker head tube angle (65.6º) provides more control when descending steep, slippery terrain
  • Steeper seat tube angle (77º degrees) provides better power transfer from the saddle for traction on loose snow.
  • Longer rear center (446 mm) for added stability in snow
  • Improved standover for easier dismounts in deep snow
  • Supports up to 100 mm travel suspension fork for more playful riding

Since its introduction as the first carbon fat-tire bike, Beargrease has inspired people to rethink what fat-tire bikes can do. The fourth-generation Beargrease features geo tweaks for improved stability, flotation over snow, and cargo and accessory configurations. It’s for riders who don’t let adverse conditions or terrain slow them down: they embrace it. If their budget allows, the carbon chassis offers lightweight, lofty riding, or a more approachable aluminum model is available for riders who prefer 27.5 wheels over 26″ and want a no-frills expedition bike.

Geometry

The Beargrease received a slacker head tube angle (65.6º), a steeper seat tube angle (77º degrees), and a longer rear center (446 mm) for added stability in snow across all sizes.

Beargrease Chassis Updates

  • Carbon fiber and 6061-T6 aluminum frame options
  • New Bearpaw carbon and aluminum forks
  • Clearance for up to 27.5 x 4.5” or 26 x 4.8” tires
  • SRAM UDH compatible
  • Cargo and accessory mounts for any adventure:
  • Top tube bag mounts
  • Direct-mount frame bag mounts under top tube on Carbon
  • Two to three bottle mounts depending on size
  • Bottle/accessory mount under downtube
  • Two sets of Three-Pack mounts on fork
  • Rear Rack compatible with use of Salsa
  • Rack-Lock Seatpost Clamp
  • Downtube fender mount

Build Options

There’s a carbon frameset only for $1,999, the aluminum complete comes in at the same, the top end is the Carbon GX AXS complete $5,999, with a Carbon Eagle 90 at $4,299 and Carbon Eagle 70 at $3,299.

See more at Salsa.
