entry.title: This Full-Suspension, Dropper-Equipped Scott E-Ville eBike Could Be the Perfect Commuter
entry.content:
Scott’s urban e-bike push just got more interesting, courtesy of an all-new E-Ville. Fresh off the Sweep commuter line launched in July around Bosch’s new Hub Line motors, Scott has unveiled the E-Ville for 2027. The new mid-drive E-Ville is a full-suspension, low step-through e-bike that borrows more from the trail than the bike lane.

Scott says the E-Ville is the one bike for everything: the grocery run, the commute, and the “I’ll just take the long way home” detour that turns into two hours. To make that work, the E-Ville gets a 6061 alloy frame with a side-extraction downtube battery, an adjustable stem, and a Syncros dropper post. Yes, a dropper on a step-through commuter, which is totally a solid idea.

The addition of a dropper to a commuter makes sitting flat-footed at stops much easier. Tap a button at the light, drop the saddle, and plant your foot like you’ve done this before.

Bosch Power for Both Models

Power comes from a Bosch Performance Line CX, which delivers up to 100Nm of torque. Battery size depends on the model: 800Wh on the E-Ville 10 SUV and 720Wh on the E-Ville 20. Both can also add a Bosch PowerMore external range extender to go further.

The ebike’s full-suspension will also be a welcome addition for some commuters, as back comfort is usually a big deal. The new E-Ville’s rear suspension is classy and clean in its tidy execution.

The rear shock is tucked inside the frame, just like on their Bold-inspired mountain bikes. So it stays out of the street grime and, ideally, out of the repair stand.

Plus, it adds a clean, fancy, and high-tech aesthetic.

You didn’t even notice that it was a full-suspension at first, did you?

Scott E-Ville 10 SUV

The 10 SUV is the more capable of the two. It gets a 120mm RockShox Recon Silver RL fork, 100mm of rear travel from an SR Suntour Raidon shock inside the frame, 60mm-wide Schwalbe Advancer all-terrain tires, a Shimano Cues 11-speed drivetrain, and a Bosch Kiox 300 display.

It comes in tawny green or peach pink.

Features

  • All-terrain tires
  • 120mm front and 100mm rear suspension travel
  • Bosch 800Wh battery
  • Bosch Kiox 300 display

The Scott E-Ville 20

The E-Ville 20 is the urban-leaning version, with 100mm front and rear travel, an SR Suntour XCM34 air fork and the same rear shock, Schwalbe Big Apple Performance tires, a 10-speed Cues drivetrain, and a Bosch Purion 200 display.

It comes in tungsten grey or silt green.

Features

  • Urban tires
  • 100mm front and rear suspension travel
  • Bosch 720Wh battery
  • Bosch Purion 200 display

Brakes, Battery, Relaxed Geometry & Bits

Both models stop with Shimano four-piston MT4120 brakes and 180mm rotors. This seems like more than adequate for a bike that can weigh over 66lbs (30kg). Scott lists claimed weights of 68.7lbs (31.16kg) for the 10 SUV and 69lbs (31.3kg) for the 20.

The E-Ville geometry seems a bit more relaxed than you’d expect from a commuter. A 66° head angle (66.5° on the 20 with the shorter travel fork), 76° seat angle, and a low bottom bracket around 326 to 331 mm should make it stable and easy to live with.

Frame sizes run S to XL, and all roll on 29-inch wheels.

The everyday stuff is covered, too: a Racktime SNAPIT 2.0 rear rack, integrated front and rear lights, full fenders, and an SP Connect phone mount integrated on top of the stem. It’s a bike built to do just about anything you can think of on a random Tuesday. It certainly looks like a great all-rounder commuter.

Scott hasn’t shared pricing or availability yet. Given the spec, expect it to sit well above entry-level commuters. We’ll update when we hear more.

OK, we got some numbers. The slightly more off-road-ready Scott E-Ville 10 SUV retails for 5400€, while the E-Ville 20 sells for 4600€. No USD pricing suggests they aren’t coming to the States any time too soon.

Hit the link for more info, as well as spec details.

Scott-Sports.com

entry.title: Suunto Race 3S In-Depth Review: A Pricey Upgrade
entry.content:
Suunto has just announced the new Suunto Race 3S, a small-form-factor watch that believes it needs a big-form-factor price increase. On top of that, Suunto has also launched a new subscription service, Suunto AI Coach, where new Suunto App features are being funneled into. I’ve been using the Suunto Race 3S over the last few weeks, and in this review I’ll dive into how it all works, and whether Suunto can justify the price.

The new Suunto Race 3S includes a brighter display, more storage, and some software feature updates that the existing Race S didn’t get this past summer. This isn’t really a major change from the previous model, but nonetheless these updates are appreciated. It also features upgraded materials, shifting from a stainless steel bezel to a titanium bezel.

In any case, I’ve been putting it through its paces over the last little bit, across all sorts of activities to see how it holds up, and how it compares to other newly announced watches from the last few weeks.

With that, let’s dive right into it!

What’s New:

Now, as you probably know, the Suunto Race 3S is an upgrade to the existing Suunto Race S. There was no Suunto Race 2S, and equally confusingly, there is no larger Suunto Race 3 companion at this point. When I asked about the Suunto Race 3 elephant in the room, Suunto simply said a variant of ‘No comment’. Thus, that elephant will stay with us for now, joining other elephants I’ll talk about later.

Of course, when you look at changes vs. the original Suunto Race S, that watch continued to get meaningful firmware updates until this past April. So I’ll ignore all of those things and focus on the new stuff otherwise (software and hardware).

Starting off with the hardware changes:

– Upgraded peak display brightness from 1,000 nits to 2,000 nits
– Upgraded lens cover material from Gorilla Glass to Sapphire Crystal glass
– Updated bezel material from stainless steel to titanium
– Upgraded optical heart rate sensor
– Faster processor (Apollo 510)
– Increased GPS time from 30 hours to 38 hours (dual-frequency), 45 hours (single-frequency)
– Increased smartwatch daily battery life from 9 days to 12 days
– Increased internal storage from 32GB to 64GB
– Added support for offline music playback (MP3 files, no streaming services)
– Increased number of SuuntoPlus apps in a single profile from 2 to 3
– Slightly increased official case size from 45mm to 46mm
– Decreased weight from 60g to 56g
– Increased retail price from $349USD to $599USD (and 349EUR to 499EUR)

Do note that while you might see NFC listed on some spec sheets, that’s only applicable for the China market. There’s no contactless payment integration elsewhere. Unfortunately, like the music streaming services piece, those industry gates closed a decade ago.

Then there are a few new software features, mainly ones that rolled out on the Suunto Race 2 this past summer:

– Added Tide Widget
– Expanded map labels (road names, water, mountain peaks)
– Added Ascent as an exercise target

Finally, Suunto has noted that there’s a new ‘Race Planner’ feature coming later this year to the Suunto Race 3S, though it’s not there at launch. Here’s a quick blurb on that:

This sounds super interesting, and so I’m keen to see how this works. Especially the pieces looking at weather. For example, does that also look at your historical training weather (e.g., if you train in cold temps, but then arrive at a hot-temp race day). And, best of all, it doesn’t require Suunto AI Coach.

Finally, when it comes to model colors, here are those three options – purple, white, and black:

With that, let’s get into the box.

In the box:

This section is pretty straightforward. Above is the Suunto Race 3S box, following the same design as other recent Suunto watches.

Below are the contents of said box:

You’ve got the band/strap, the pod (separated from the band), the braided charging cable, and some paper stuff.

The charging cable follows other recent Suunto models, and is magnetic and much better than the one that came with the original Suunto S model, which I found would often become misaligned.

In any case, you simply embark on a 10-15-second IKEA assembly project to attach the standard band straps to the watch pod, and you’re off and running.

The Basics:

In this section, I’m going to look at some of the basics of the watch, including daily usage such as activity tracking, sleep, etc. As well as pieces like responsiveness and general usability.

The Suunto Race 3S has a three-button layout, as well as a touchscreen. You can mostly use either touch or buttons for navigating around the user interface. The upper right button accesses the sport menu, the middle Digital Crown allows access to pinned widgets during smartwatch use (and of course scrolls up/down), and the bottom button acts as a back/escape button.

The left side has no buttons. Meanwhile, the touchscreen is a 2,000-nit display that’s perfectly viewable in both bright sunny conditions or shade conditions. I live on a Mediterranean island, and I’ve had no issues viewing the display in any scenarios out on the trails. Oh, for fun, here are three watches side-by-side: Suunto Race S, Suunto Race 2, and Suunto Race 3S

That said, it can’t be left unstated that virtually all watches released in 2026 are using 3,000-nit panels. The COROS Pace 4 Pro released a few weeks ago is using a 3,500-nit display (which is also larger), and atop that, the more-capable watch is $150 cheaper. To be super clear here, I have no issue with seeing the display at all. Period, hard-stop. However, we can’t ignore the fact that Suunto is putting in kinda old tech but with over-the-top premium prices. To me, the ‘savings’ on this display panel should be reflected in the price. It’s clearly not.

The only minor ‘nit’-picking I’d have with the display is that their power-saving algorithms seem a little bit aggressive at times, quickly dimming the panel within a few seconds of wrist-raise. Again, the display is still visible, but this could use a bit of work.

Speaking of brightness, note that for whatever weird reason, there’s no physical LED flashlight like there is in the Suunto Vertical 2 watch (which is priced the same at $599). You still have a screen-based flashlight, but obviously that’s not the same.

Perhaps given Suunto’s lawsuit with Garmin concerning the topic, they got a bit skittish. Either way, it’s a bit of a bummer.

In any case, scrolling down into the widgets, you’ve got a customizable set of quick-access data bits. I will note that if you watch the video, you’ll see it’s more laggy here than the older Suunto Race S – despite the claims of a faster processor. This is such a good example of why processor specs mean absolutely nothing in most devices. You can have the fastest processor in the world, but if the firmware/operating system isn’t optimized for it, it’ll still be slower than an optimized processor. Again, check out the above video for that.

As for those widgets, they all work just as before. Aside from the new Tides one, there’s nothing new here. You can tap into any given smaller widget in this list to open up details about that topic, such as steps, sleep, weather, etc.

When it comes to things like sleep tracking, the times I went to sleep and woke up have largely been correct here, usually matching the other wearables within a few minutes. The same goes for the HRV status values. I don’t compare sleep phases/stages, because doing so is peak faux-science. The best-case reference devices you can use to do so are only about 80% accurate, which isn’t all that great (and again, that’s a best-case scenario in perfect lab conditions). Thus, we’d never compare a heart rate sensor to a chest strap that was wrong 20% of the time. Therefore, I’m not gonna do it here either.

Meanwhile, most of the data around heart rate-driven metrics comes from the new optical heart rate sensor seen on the bottom. As I’ll show you within the accuracy section, this heart rate sensor is a huge jump up over the previous Suunto Race S sensor, which wasn’t super awesome.

Speaking of other internal-ish things, the unit now has 64GB of internal storage, which is ostensibly mostly for offline music (yes, it’s also for maps, but Suunto’s maps are so well optimized that you simply don’t need anywhere near that much storage…more on that in the next section).

Now, with Suunto’s offline music playback, it requires you to transfer MP3 files via USB cable to the device. There are no offline streaming services (e.g., Spotify/etc), and that’s simply not going to happen anytime soon. Those industry gates closed nearly a decade ago now, and the only way Suunto would gain access to them is by going back to WearOS. Nonetheless, if you’re one of 12 people who are still transferring your owned/“borrowed” MP3 files to your watch via cable, you can do that here. You’ll pair up any Bluetooth audio device (e.g., headphones) to the watch, and off you go. It all worked pretty easily for me, and you can also load in playlists as well.

Finally, when it comes to smartphone notifications, you’ll get the basic text and emoji from your phone.

Ok, with all that sorted, let’s get into the sports bits.

Sports Usage & Mapping:

Next up, we’ve got all things sports, including mapping and navigation.

To access a sport mode, you’ll tap the upper right button, which opens up the workout panel. Here it’ll automatically open your last sport mode, and start searching for GPS (if outside), as well as get heart rate lock. Further, if you’ve got paired sensors (like cycling sensors or an external heart rate sensor), it’ll pair to those too.

You can change the sport mode to one of a boatload of other sport modes in the list:

Back on that main page though, you can select to load a course (within Navigation), as well as select/load SuuntoPlus apps. The Suunto Race 3S supports up to three concurrent enabled SuuntoPlus apps within a given sport profile (you can have additional apps loaded but not enabled). In addition, you can also load up ‘Guides’, which would include things like structured workouts. However, you can only load two apps + one concurrent guide, if using guides.

Finally, there are also the exercise options, where you can tweak various display, map, and other target settings. For example, the Suunto Race 3S added the ability to set an Ascent target (similar to how you might set a calorie or distance target). This came in a firmware update for other newer Suunto watches this summer, but the existing Suunto Race S was skipped.

In any case, circling back, I’m gonna add a course to navigate for my trail run. So I’ll select that back in the Navigation/Routes area:

In terms of maps, the Suunto Race 3S doesn’t have any maps pre-loaded, though they are easily downloadable via WiFi from Suunto. You simply go into the app and choose the regions you want. Here are some random sizes to get a feel for things:

Since I’m here, one thing I really wish Suunto would sort out is their app to watch syncing/configuration situation. For years it’s been that as soon as the watch thinks you want to tweak something, it starts syncing, which in turn prohibits you from actually tweaking the thing until it’s done, taking forever to do that. It’s just very 1990s-modal style. I can’t think of a single other wearable device that still has that restriction left. And more critically, there’s no way to cancel the app from syncing once it starts. That’d at least half-way solve it.

It’s in this area of the app that you’d modify things like the data fields/pages of your sport modes, add new SuuntoPlus apps, create interval workouts, and more. Of course, like in the past, you still can’t modify default sports profiles; you have to create a new custom one if you want to tweak something. And it needs to sync a bunch back and forth too. These are the types of actual useful things I wished Suunto would focus on, rather than adding offline MP3 music support that virtually nobody will use.

With that all sorted, synced, and re-synced, we’re ready to start our workout. Off I go for a run. While running, I’ll of course see my data pages as configured:

From a navigation standpoint, I’ll get a little chirp and then an on-screen notification when a turn comes up. And then if I miss a turn, I’ll get a notification about that too, such as this:

Otherwise, the route shows as expected, and in terms of the responsiveness of the map, it’s a double-edged sword. For rotation, things were instant, and I didn’t experience any black square tiles. You can see this in the video.

But for zooming in/out, there was always at least a second or two of black square tiles. Ironically, a runner friend was with me as I was sitting there filming this, and not being familiar with Suunto watches, he was a bit surprised and asked “Is that normal?”

And ultimately, different companies handle things in different ways. For Garmin, when it slow-map renders, it has a fuzzy look or other color-matching tiles (or shows a tile at a higher zoom level first, before enumerating the detailed tile). Most other companies do the same. But in Suunto’s case, they’re just showing black tiles, which looks a bit sloppy.

Even more so, because I’d also notice these tiles as I run, if I had the map screen just open. Meaning, visible at a glance on my wrist even when not fully raised. Again, we can have an academic debate on slow-map-loading differences (more detail vs less detail, etc.), but I think we can all agree that the black tiles just look rough.

In any case, you’ll also be able to see your progress on the elevation and climbs, both for the full course, and then specific climbs as you trip them:

All of this worked perfectly fine. After the workout, you’ll get a summary of your workout as expected on the watch:

And then likewise you’ll see the additional detail within the Suunto App:

Assuming you have your account connected to one of Suunto’s boatload of partners (e.g., Strava, TrainingPeaks, etc.), it’ll automatically push that data off to those platforms. Again, all of that worked without issue for me.

So then, let’s talk about the accuracy of that data.

Accuracy of Heart Rate & GPS:

The new Suunto Race 3S has a new optical heart rate sensor compared to the existing Suunto Race S. Suunto says this new sensor has six LEDs and four photodetectors behind 2.5D curved sensor glass. No matter what it has behind it, I’ll just state things up front: It’s really darn good in my testing.

I’ll also cover the GNSS/GPS side of things, as well as battery and elevation bits down below. But the GNSS piece hasn’t changed here, so we’ll keep that efficient.

Let’s start off with this slightly hilly run I did. It started off with a long and occasionally steep descent, before some flats, and then going all the way back up again. As a reminder, hills (going down), can often be challenging for optical HR sensors. Still, the Suunto nailed it here. I’ve got zero complaints.

Next, we’ve got a 90-minute long trail run across plenty of varied terrain (steep stuff, shallow stuff, rocking spicy stuff, etc.). And again, overall very good.

About the only thing I could nitpick here is this section for about 20 seconds, where it’s off by about 3-5bpm. That’s nothing in a 98-minute long workout. Again, really good job here.

Here’s another trail run from yesterday. Setting aside whatever happened with the chest strap at the 28-minute marker for a few seconds, things here were quite good as well. Again, there’s virtually nothing to be upset about, and this also included some steep ups/downs.

Next, just for fun, check out this shorter morning gravel ride thing I did a few days ago. I was taking photos and such on this ride of a few different devices. So lots of stop-and-go. Lots of pretty spicy typical Mallorca gravel chunk (most would call it MTB material). And yet, it absolutely nails this. Like, really solid job while cycling.

Now, I’m going to continue to test this sensor, but switch over to the new Suunto Run 2 sensor over the coming weeks, so stay tuned for that. I don’t expect a difference though. Either way, this represents a major improvement for Suunto over past sensors.

Meanwhile, on the GPS side, let’s quickly run through some of these. Here’s that city run from a few nights ago. At a high level, obviously all look pretty good.

Meanwhile, in the actual city/downtown parts with tall buildings, none of the units did amazing. None were bad, but across the board (Garmin, Suunto, Apple), all of them were ‘blah’ accuracy-wise. I’m not quite sure why.

You can see this here as well. Again, nothing was crazy-bad, but all four units took turns crashing through buildings slightly, cutting corners, and generally acting like the drunk tourists that fill this area.

That said, as soon as I left the buildings behind, it was perfectly fine on the rest of the run:

Moving along, looking at yesterday’s trail run, which includes cliffs, ravines, trees, etc., things at a high level look good:

I could quibble about each unit being a few meters offset at different parts of the route. Here the Fenix 9 Pro briefly goes across the road, then the COROS and Suunto do the same some 20 seconds later.

Still, we’re talking less than a 5-meter difference in most cases, such as this here:

Or going around this gate for cars. The Garmin & Suunto were most correct here; the COROS went a bit more lazily around it.

Anyway, this is the pattern over and over again – basically all these units were spot on across runs, rides, etc. I’ve got some actual swim tests to do this weekend (I’ve spent a bunch of time in the water swimming with it, but wasn’t doing accuracy testing).

As for looking at the elevation, no major concerns on any of my activities. Here’s that 90-minute trail run:

This is the one I showed the other day in the Garmin MARQ Gen3 review, where for some reason both Garmin units started sliding downwards while I stood and took some photos (27min marker). Garmin’s already digging into it, as it’s likely firmware-related if two different units do it. I will say there’s a little bit of separation early on in the above that seems a bit odd between the Suunto/COROS and the Apple/Garmin watches. Though those all eventually bundled back up together again.

As for the battery bits, here’s the official battery chart:

Looking at my battery life in always-on display, with roughly 60-90mins of GPS time per day, I’m closer to about 5ish days, maybe a touch bit more, but a little shy of the 7-day above (which is spec’d as 60mins per day, versus my times a bit higher). Also, my routes had navigation enabled, which would draw more battery.

Speaking of which, looking at that 98-minute trail run, you can see it burned about 5%, putting me on a 28-hour battery estimate in dual-frequency/multiband mode. This is a touch bit lower than the always-on specs above, but again remember I did have navigation enabled, which draws more battery.

Also, kudos to Suunto for including battery data in their .FIT files (Garmin, Wahoo, and others do so, though unfortunately COROS does not).

In any case, in terms of all my accuracy bits, I’m good across the board here; I’ve got no concerns in any category. Again, for the heart rate sensor side, this is a big upgrade.

Suunto AI Coach Subscription:

Next, Suunto has announced a new Suunto AI Coach subscription feature, which let’s you use your current and historical Suunto data to get race planning information and tons more. This feature is launching on/with the Suunto Race 3S, though it is expected to go to other watch user bases. It’s currently fully on the app itself, as there’s no on-device component.

Suunto has a pretty good 10-minute video that explains the boatload of features that exist there.

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

My one (kinda big) quibble here is that Suunto Race 3S users get 3 months free to the service, yet Suunto hasn’t defined what said service will actually cost once that free trial ends. And somehow that rubs me the wrong way. Perhaps it’s because my inbox is filled with AI vibe-coded slop apps that often attempt to hook you into the platform before eventually charging you down the road. In this case, Suunto is clear they’ll be charging you eventually, but aren’t saying what that is. Thus, once you get hooked on it, you’ll feel compelled to start paying for it.

Now mind you, what Suunto is offering certainly seems a heck of a lot more compelling than what Amazfit, Garmin, and others are doing. It doesn’t seem as deep as what Fitbit/Google are doing, but again, we don’t know Suunto’s pricing yet. Suunto says that part of the reason they haven’t decided pricing is because they want to see what people actually use, and get feedback. Which is fair enough, but still seems like something they could have done before they launched it.

Now, despite my annoyance with Suunto’s AI Coach rollout, I will give them all the credit in the world that they’ve also announced a new Suunto MCP that’ll be free for all Suunto users. This joins COROS in offering such a thing for free. I have a feeling we’re going to see similar announcements in the near future from others. Note that in the case of Suunto’s MCP, the details are thin at this point, other than it’ll be free, and it’ll exist. Still, I take both of those for the moment.

Wrap-Up:

Suunto has had a string of solid product launches over the last couple of years, paired with frequent and meaningful firmware/feature updates on the app side. And good expansion on the developer side. They’ve been on a roll across the board. But I struggle to put the Suunto Race 3S in that category of wins. This watch feels…off.

To begin, the biggest issue is the price. At $599USD/499EUR, it’s more than a 70% USD price increase over the launch price of the Suunto Race S just two years ago. And it’s not like they’ve drastically changed the hardware. Sure, it has a brighter 2,000-nit display panel, but that panel is what other companies were putting in their watches two years ago, not the 3,000-3,500-nit panels that companies are putting in watches in 2026. Further, while they increased the storage from 32GB to 64GB, it doesn’t really serve any meaningful purpose. Suunto’s maps are tiny in size, and easily fit within even just 16GB of space. And while in theory the extra space is for music playback, the reality is virtually nobody is downloading MP3s to their watches in 2026 (since Suunto doesn’t support offline music from any streaming service). Plus, where are the other hardware features that other companies are putting in their watches for half the price (e.g., flashlights, voice, microphone & proper speaker, etc.)?

After a string of wins, I think Suunto missed the boat on this one. It feels both overpriced, and kinda seems like it’s just a collection of leftover hardware parts, rather than representing the start of a new Race 3 series generation of watches. Perhaps if it was priced at $399 or at most $449, I’d feel differently. But with the just-released COROS Pace 4 Pro being at $449, that’s a very tough spot for Suunto to be competing in with the specs they have in the Race 3S.

With that, thanks for reading.

entry.title: ‘A Dictatorship’: Team Picnic-PostNL Rocked by Allegations of Culture of Fear

entry.title: Le Pilgrimage Gravel 2026: Sharing the Journey – Simon Rosmolen, Cyril Chermin, Yorit Kluitman, & Gjis Ferkranus
entry.content:
Le Pilgrimage is a journey through the French and Italian Alps, shaped by the trails, the food, and the people you meet along the way. It is about taking time to stop, share a table, notice where you are, and let the experience unfold at its own pace. This fourth edition once again showed how much happens in the moments between the climbs.

 

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start"><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start"></span></span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start"></span>

 

For the fourth time, about fifty pilgrims gathered in Puy-Saint-Vincent from around ten different countries to share some of the best trails, food and company the Écrins area has to offer. Le Pilgrimage sold out within 24 hours, but what makes the event stand out is the contrast between demanding days in the mountains and the comfort of Hotel Saint Roch, where everyone returns to the same table at the end of the day.

Le Pilgrimage is deliberately not a race. There is no ranking, no timing, and no prize for being first. It is not about speed, watts, calories, or shaving minutes off the day. The focus is on the experience itself: the places you stop, the people you meet, the food you share and the time you spend in the landscape.

The event kicks off with a communal dinner where all pilgrims gather at long tables, sitting next to total strangers, chatting mostly about their set-up, previous rides, or what they expect. Over the next four days, the route repeatedly creates reasons to stop and spend time together. Sometimes that means sitting down for fondue at a checkpoint, sometimes following a paper map to a hidden cabin, stopping at a bakery, or simply returning to the same table at basecamp at the end of the day.

Stage 1: Starting close to home

Day one is all about getting to know the area and each other, so route designer and founder Simon Rosmolen keeps the route quite close to basecamp, following the Durance Valley, taking on the Réotier climb and finishing with the Pousterle climb, which is practically the backyard of the hotel.

After just 38 kilometres, the riders reach the first checkpoint where, besides their first stamp, they also find a long lunch table in the middle of an alpine meadow with cheese fondue, white wine, and local cheeses and sausages. Riders are invited to relax, sit down, enjoy the food and amazing views instead of just rushing on. The checkpoints are designed to slow riders down.

There is even a bonus challenge in the shape of a printed map that takes riders further up to an isolated cabin where patron Saint Roch has left a message and some more local delicacies for them. That night, the volume at the dinner table is already notably higher than on the first night.

Stage 2: Back to Fort Janus

After a hearty breakfast buffet, the riders line up on the local ski slope with another highlight in their sights: Fort Janus. This defensive structure from the last century is now just a crumbling ruin with breathtaking 360º views of the surrounding valleys in both France and Italy. Along the way, they first tackle another climb above Saint-Martin-de-Queyrières before descending towards Briançon and our favourite bakery, where riders happily stop to sample the croissants, pains aux raisins,  and baguettes. Most fill up their bags or jerseys for the long climb ahead to the fort.

Most riders need at least 1.5 hours to reach the summit, where the organisers await them with crêpes with Nutella, local génépi and a well-deserved second stamp. And, not to forget, time to simply stand still and take in the almost absurd view across the French-Italian borderlands from 2,500 metres.

Stage 3A: Into Piedmont

After two glorious sunny days, the queen stage starts with an overcast sky and the promise of rain. Besides the weather, the route also looks more challenging as the organisers try to build up during the event. This also means the riders have to find and book their own accommodation and dinner as the route dives into the Piemonte area.

To get there, they have to ascend the Col de Bousson, an ancient smugglers’ route with the border at the summit. Most riders climb in pouring rain and are happy to find lighter skies on the Italian side of the border when they descend into a valley where time seems to have stood still.

Most riders opt to enjoy lunch in the rifugio before they hit the ski town of Sestrière and climb further up to the infamous Strada dell’Assietta. This high alpine military road is now home to adventurers of all shapes and sizes. Tremendous views open up high above the valleys, and this year the riders only ride about 15 kilometres of this gravel road before enjoying one of the best descents of the journey, flowing through the woods for many kilometres down to Bardonecchia.

There, the call of pizza is answered by almost all riders but one. Tom Rijnders chooses to bivvy out on the climb towards the Colle del Sommeiller, a climb that somehow manages to scare and inspire at the same time.

The final chapter of the journey is a crescendo to remember. The dead-end gravel climb up to nearly 3,000 metres passes wild pastures and steep rock faces, along a trail that gets rougher and rougher the closer you get to the summit. It might not be particularly steep, but climbing for 24 kilometres is never easy, especially when the temperature at the top is a meagre four degrees Celsius.

Almost all riders make it to the small shelter at the top, where Saint Roch, or San Rocco on this side of the border, has left a final message and some food for the riders, asking them to reflect on their ride and share what they will remember from these four days of riding in the Alps.

What remains is a long descent back down the Sommeiller towards Rifugio Scarfiotti. There, on a plateau partway down the mountain, the third and final stamp is waiting, together with a traditional Italian buffet prepared by Daisy, the rifugista, and her welcoming team at the refuge. The meal proves to be a welcome refuel, because the ride back to basecamp turns out to be tougher than it looked on paper.

The distance itself is manageable, but the weather has other plans. A local hailstorm with thunder and lightning circles around Briançon and follows some of the riders almost all the way back up to Puy-Saint-Vincent.

The Final Arrivals

By the end of the day, most pilgrims are already back at basecamp. But some of the most memorable scenes come just before dinner, when the final two riders appear at the hotel. All the pilgrims who had already finished are waiting to welcome Anne and Bruce home. The biggest applause of the week is reserved for those arriving last, in recognition of their effort and for completing their own pilgrimage.

And perhaps those last riders have, in some ways, experienced the route most fully. They have spent the longest time outside, the longest time on the trail, and maybe the longest time simply being present in the journey.

With everyone safely back at basecamp, the pilgrims gather for one final dinner. Later that night, in the bar of Hotel Saint Roch, none of the riders feels much urge to head to bed early. New friendships are celebrated, stories shared, and Instagram handles and phone numbers exchanged.

Within just four days, fifty strangers have shared an experience that will stay with them. Not just the routes and places along the way, but also the conversations, helping each other and sharing this journey.

Le Pilgrimage Bikepacking

Next year, Le Pilgrimage turns five. Alongside a new basecamp edition, there will also be a new multi-day bikepacking edition. The format will be different, but the ingredients will remain the same: a shared dinner before departure, one long multi-day route with checkpoints designed to slow riders down, and one big final dinner where everyone comes back together to share the stories of the road. More info at Le pilgrimage.

Le Pilgrimage Gravel 2027

The fifth edition of Le Pilgrimage Gravel at Basecamp Hotel Saint Roch will return in 2027. Four days of riding through the Alps, with a basecamp to return to, checkpoints along the way, and the Pilgrims’ Table at the end of each day. Dates will be announced soon.

The post Le Pilgrimage Gravel 2026: Sharing the Journey appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Revel Bikes Introduces the Ranger Ti, Its First Production Ti Full-Suspension Model
entry.content:
Today, Revel Bikes introduced the Ranger Ti, its first production titanium full-suspension model. It’s essentially an exact copy of the latest carbon Ranger V3, but combines the carbon rear triangle and links with a new titanium front triangle that includes a 3D-printed head tube, bottom bracket, and pivot junctions. The goal was to combine the damped ride quality of titanium with the lateral stiffness of the carbon rear triangle to create a unique version of its popular short-travel bike.

Revel says, “The Ranger Ti isn’t lighter, cheaper, or easier to make, and that’s kind of the point.” Instead, it’s meant to be a unique combination of materials, engineering, and manufacturing techniques that showcase the brand’s decade of titanium experience and expertise in producing carbon mountain bikes in a darn good-looking package.

Ranger Ti Details

Many readers are probably already aware that Revel’s founding team also launched Why Cycles in 2016 to specialize in titanium mountain, fat bike, and gravel frames. Why Cycles and Revel officially merged in 2023, and the titanium program has continued. Last year, Revel showed us Project RaTical, a full-suspension Ti prototype, and told us all about its Experimental Concept Labs last spring. And who could forget the most recent example, the El Jefe Grande 32” titanium hardtail that just launched last week.

Now, Revel is taking that experience and applying it to the Ranger Ti frame. It’s essentially the same bike as the Ranger V3, just with a slick-looking titanium front triangle. Using advanced 3D-printing technology, Revel printed the head tube, bottom bracket, and pivot junctions to remove the construction challenges and limitations of traditional welding and create the smooth lines of the Ranger Ti frame. These 3D-printed parts are then sleeved at their junctions and welded to titanium tubing. Revel says the frames are third-party ISO tested “and represent true limits of materials engineering, 3D printing, and titanium fabrication.” 

The CBF (Canfiled Balance Formula) suspension design joins the titanium front triangle to the carbon rear triangle and links. The same suspension travel (120mm rear / 130mm front) and kinematics that make the Ranger V3 a popular short-travel mountain bike carry over, as does the downcountry-oriented geometry. It’s worth mentioning that the titanium front triangle adds a bit of weight compared to the full-carbon version, with the frame weighing 8.02 lbs in size large, and the complete XO build with NOBL/Bird wheels and Pike/Super Deluxe Ultimate suspension weighing in around 29.5 pounds.

Ranger Ti Features

  • Shared geometry and kinematics with Ranger V3
  • Shared carbon rear triangle and links
  • Four bottle/utility mounts on sizes M through XL, three on Small
  • Long dropper post insertion
  • Custom rubber chainstay protection
  • Debris fender
  • UDH compatible
  • Full internal routing
  • Frame weight: 8.02 lbs, size Large (3.64kg)

Want One?

Revel is introducing the Ranger Ti in an extremely limited first-batch run of just 10 numbered frames, which are scheduled to ship in December. It appears that in this first batch, the small and large frames have already sold out, but reservations can still be made for Feb/March delivery. 

The Ranger Ti frame set retails for $5,969, and you can reserve yours for $500 down. Four complete build options are available, ranging in price from $7,969 for SRAM Eagle 90, topping out at $14,169 for the SRAM XX Transmission Flight Attendant kit. You can learn more about the Ranger Ti or reserve yours today on the Revel Bikes website.

revelbikes.com

entry.title: Wolf Tooth’s SHIFT Pedals Now Available in Limited-Edition Camo at Dealers Only
entry.content:
Wolf Tooth Components believes that bike shops are the cornerstone of the bike industry. To back that up, Wolf Tooth tells us they started a new dealer program this year, and part of that commitment involves developing some exclusive, dealer-only products and limited editions. The Camo SHIFT Gravity Pedals are the first of these products to be produced in a limited run of just 150 pairs and available only through brick-and-mortar retailers. Wolf Tooth says that moving forward, it expects one or two dealer-exclusive products to be released each year.

Camo SHIFT Gravity Pedals

Wolf Tooth completed its family of clipless pedals earlier this year when it launched the SHIFT Gravity Pedals. This added a large platform model alongside the CTRL (trail), ALT (XC), and DEL (gravel race) models that came out last year. Now, the SHIFT is the first product to get the dealer-exclusive treatment in a limited-edition Camo colorway.

Based in Minnesota, Wolf Tooth says the fall colors are in full swing, so it makes sense to launch a camouflage pedal now. They worked with Ashley Anodized It (@ashley.anodized.it on Instagram) to create the one-of-a-kind camo finishes on the pedal bodies. According to Wolf Tooth, “Each pedal body features a unique anodized camouflage pattern in olive, tan, black, and brown tones, finished off with a blaze orange end cap, because when you go all in, you go all in.”

Where Can I Buy Camo SHIFT Pedals?

Wolf Tooth says that they pre-sold 130 pairs of Camo SHIFT Pedals to dealers. They have a landing page on their website with a dealer locator showing only the dealers with inventory of the Camo SHIFT pedals; check it out here. According to Wolf Tooth, they aren’t allowing any online sale of the Camo SHIFT Pedals; customers need to visit the shop (or call) to order a pair. The idea is to drive traffic to the shops that are so instrumental to our cycling communities.

Don’t see your LBS or another shop near you on the list? Wolf Tooth says it intentionally held back 20 pairs of the Camo pedals so any shop can order them for you, on a first-come, first-served basis. All the shop needs to do is reach out to Wolf Tooth’s dealer support team.

Pricing and Availability

The limited-edition dealer-exclusive Camo SHIFT Pedals retail for $289.95 and are available now at select retailers nationwide. Head to the SHIFT dealer locator here to find the nearest location with stock of the Camo pedals, or hit up your LBS to order you a pair before they’re gone. And if you head to the Wolf Tooth website, be sure to check out the limited-edition Camo merch; they’ve got hats and long-sleeve T-shirts.

wolftoothcomponents.com

entry.title: Revel Bikes Announces the Ranger Ti
entry.content:
Revel Bikes today released the Ranger Ti, the company’s first production full suspension frame built around a titanium front triangle. The frame pairs this new front end with the carbon rear triangle and links from the Ranger V3 while maintaining the same geometry and kinematics.

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start"><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start"></span></span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start"></span>

 

Titanium has been a part of Revel since before its inception. The founding team launched Why Cycles in 2016 to build modern titanium bikes. Why merged with Revel in 2023, and the titanium program has run continuously since, producing hardtails, gravel bikes, and most recently the El Jefe Grande. Revel showed their Project RaTical under their Concept Labs umbrella last summer, in their first public showing of their experimentation with 3D printing and titanium full suspension. The Ranger Ti is the culmination of all those efforts and is their first production titanium full suspension platform.

Geometry and kinematics carry straight over from the carbon Ranger V3. Higher anti-squat and higher progression keep the Ranger’s downcountry intent intact: efficient pedaling, active suspension, and a supportive, bottomless feel through the travel. A steep seat tube angle, slightly longer reach, slack head angle, and lower bottom bracket round out a geometry built for long days and confident descents.

Revel Ranger Ti Quick Hits

  • Shared geometry and kinematics with Ranger V3 Carbon
  • Shared carbon rear triangle and links
  • Four bottle/utility mounts on sizes M through XL, three on S
  • Long dropper post insertion
  • Custom rubber chainstay protection
  • Debris fender
  • UDH compatible
  • Full internal cable routing
  • Frame weight: 8.02lbs size Large (3.64kg)
  • Complete bike as shown: 29.5lb size Large (13.38kg)

Why 3D printed Titanium?

Revel used the most advanced 3D printing technology for the headtube, upper shock mount, bottom bracket, and pivot interfaces on the front triangle. This has allowed Revel to leverage the shape not only for aesthetics, but also to accomplish things traditional machining and forging cannot. Welding titanium and putting multiple pivot points in precise locations can be super tough, and create either a bike that is too heavy, not strong enough, or sacrifces on the kinematics because pivot points had construction limitations. 3D printing removes that, and allows Revel to use its “carbon engineering oversight” to make a titanium bike with all the modern features of a carbon frame. Stiff 3D printed junctions are sleeved and then welded to titanium tubing to optimize the supple ride feel of titanium and strength of 3D printing. The frames are third party ISO tested in California and represent true limits of materials engineering, 3D printing, and titanium fabrication. All combining with Revel’s carbon expertise and pivot hardware/bearing interface to make a bike that rides incredibly well.

Pricing and Availability

The first batch of Ranger Ti frames is limited to 10 pieces, individually numbered, and available for reservation now, with an expected ship date before the end of the year.

Framesets are priced at $5,969 at revelbikes.com and £4999 at revelbikes.uk

Complete builds are also available.

The post Revel Bikes Announces the Ranger Ti appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: State Bicycle Co 6061 Trail+ Fat Bike V2
entry.content:
New for the 26/27 winter riding season, State Bicycle Co brings back a classic: its 6061 Trail+ Fat Bike, now updated to V2…

State’s Fat Bike hasn’t received a substantial update in a decade. The new model joins the State Trail Family as the Trail+ Fat Bike v2, featuring an all-new hydroformed 6061 aluminum frame, modern geometry, and specs ready for winter and desert riding.

Highlights include the 66º head tube angle, UDH compatibility, Carbon Fork Upgrade, mounts galore, and Tektro hydraulic brakes with 180 rotors. The Shimano drivetrain offers a whopping 409% range in a durable, price-conscious package. Fat bikes are ridden where cadence collapses: soft sand, deep snow, loaded climbs. Range matters, gear count doesn’t. Complete bikes start at just over 1K, keeping with State’s ethos of accessible bikes for all riders.

This is a completely new frame, with a much slacker front end and hydraulic brakes. The 6061 Trail+ v2 trades its predecessor’s conservative numbers for a 66° head angle, 455 mm chainstays, and a 50mm stem on a 740 mm bar — modern trail geometry applied to a fat bike. It rolls on Kenda Juggernaut 26 x 4.5″ tires, with room for 4.8″

Specs:

  • $1,199.99
  • 26 x 4.8″ clearance
  • Geometry — all sizes
  • Head tube angle: 66°
  • Seat tube angle: 74°
  • Chainstay / rear center: 455mm
  • Bottom bracket drop: 65mm
  • Fork offset: 45mm
  • Fork axle-to-crown: 485mm
  • Trail: ~109mm

Check out more at State Bicycle Co.

entry.title: Adventure Cycling Association Launches the Eastern Canada Bicycle Route: 930 Miles Linking Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City
entry.content:
Adventure Cycling Association‘s newest route, the Eastern Canada Bicycle Route, is 930 miles long, linking Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City…

The new Eastern Canada Bicycle Route route runs 65% on bike paths and multi-use trails, offering an approachable international bike tour without a long-haul flight.

Eastern Canada Bicycle Route

Adventure Cycling Association, a leading U.S. bicycle-travel nonprofit, launched the Eastern Canada Route, a 930-mile (1,500 km) bicycle route through southern Ontario and Québec. It connects four of eastern Canada’s most iconic cities: Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City. It is Adventure Cycling’s second route, and longest, entirely within the country.

The route runs 65% on bike paths and multi-use trails and is roughly 40% unpaved.

Three research riders physically rode every section in June and July 2026. They checked surface conditions, navigation, safety, and services along the way.

The route is split into three roughly equal sections. Each starts and ends in a major city with air, rail, and bus connections, so riders can tackle the full tour or a single section.

Built on the Trans Canada Trail and La Route Verte

The Eastern Canada Bicycle Route was inspired by two trail networks built by Canadian organizations, communities, and volunteers. The Trans Canada Trail (Sentier Transcanadien) is the world’s longest multi-use trail system, and the route highlights one of its
most popular stretches. La Route Verte, Québec’s provincial cycling network stewarded by Vélo Québec, is one of the longest interconnected cycling networks in North America.

“The Eastern Canada Bicycle Route builds on some of the best cycling infrastructure in North America, created by Canadian communities and organizations like the Trans Canada Trail and Vélo Québec. We utilized the best infrastructure for cycling between Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City, had our research riders test every section, and added detailed navigation and services information. This route is an important part of our growth in serving bicycle travel across North America, and it’s a great eastern counterpart to our Vancouver Crossing Loop and the Canadian section of the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route in the west.” said Jeffrey Mizell, director of routes at Adventure Cycling Association.

Adventure Cycling built on the work of these local organizations, using its 50 years of expertise in creating long distance bike routes to create a specific and unique experience for traveling cyclists. It chose routing suited to loaded touring, added detailed navigation, and documented services, lodging, and riding conditions for every section.

“The Eastern Canada Bicycle Route is an inviting introduction to long-distance bike touring, with manageable terrain, well-spaced services, and an abundance of dedicated bike paths. Whether you’re new to multi-day touring or a seasoned cyclist looking for a rewarding adventure, this route offers an approachable way to experience the landscapes, communities, and culture of eastern Canada,” says Amy Wally, Cartography Program Manager.

Section Highlights

Section 1: Toronto to Ottawa (364 miles / 586 km; 45% bike path, 50% unpaved). Riders leave Canada’s largest city over the Oak Ridges Moraine, then follow crushed-limestone rail trails through Uxbridge, Lindsay, and Peterborough. The route crosses Doube’s
Trestle Bridge and the Ranney Gorge Suspension Bridge, then enters the lakes and forests of the Canadian Shield via remote roads and the K&P Trail. It reaches the national capital through Perth, Smiths Falls, and Carleton Place.

Section 2: Ottawa to Montréal (290 miles / 467 km; 70% bike path, 20% unpaved). The Main Route heads north through Gatineau Valley into the Laurentians through Wakefield and Maniwaki, then routes to Le P’tit Train du Nord, a 145-mile (234 km) former
railway corridor. A more direct River Alternate follows the Ottawa River and Route Verte 1 past Oka National Park.

Section 3: Montréal to Québec City (273 miles / 439 km; 85% bike path, 50% unpaved). From Montréal’s bike network, the route follows the Chambly Canal and La Route Verte through Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Granby, Magog, and Sherbrooke. It then crosses
Québec’s quiet agricultural heartland and finishes with a ferry across the St. Lawrence River into Québec City.

About the Trans Canada Trail

The Trans Canada Trail is the longest multi-use trail system in the world and is always growing. It reaches every province and territory and connects all three of Canada’s coastlines. Each section of the Trans Canada Trail is managed locally and supports different
activities and community needs.

As an organization, the Trans Canada Trail advocates for, stewards, and champions Canada’s nationwide trail system. It is a registered charity that receives funding from the Government of Canada (through Parks Canada), various provincial, territorial, and municipal
governments, and generous donors.

Riders can learn more about the Trans Canada Trail and ways to support it at tctrail.ca and La Route Verte at routeverte.com.

Availability

The Eastern Canada Route is available now as a digital route. Riders navigate with Adventure Cycling’s digital route through Ride with GPS, with riding conditions, services, and points of interest for each section. Visit Adventure Cycling for more.

entry.title: Neuhaus Metalworks Solstice Hardtail Review: Nothing More, Nothing Less – John Watson & Kyle Klain
entry.content:
Ever since his 2023 Shop Visit, in which he first laid eyes on the Neuhaus Solstice prototype, John has wanted to get his grubby mitts on one to ride. Once the production run of frames landed from Taiwan, the team at Neuhaus Metalworks sent a Solstice frame, fork, and brakes out for him to build up. He took this opportunity to build the ideal metal hardtail; nothing more, nothing less…

Looking back to over three years ago, I had just wrapped up a ride in China Camp with Nick Neuhaus aboard a size XL Hummingbird hardtail. We’d done one of Nick’s favorite loops and were resting by a picturesque tree, surrounded by California poppies, talking shop. Nick’s partner with Neuhaus, Daniel Yang, was just getting over a cold, so he couldn’t ride with us, but he met up after the ride, and with him, he brought his Solstice prototype hardtail.

At the time, all Neuhaus frames were made in California, but since that 2023 Shop Visit, Neuhaus has moved to manufacturing its “Core” line in Taiwan. This includes a Core Hummingbird and Core Solstice. Nick still builds custom bikes out of his Novato-based shop.

The XC-oriented Hummingbird, left, and the more trail-ready Solstice, right…

While the 120 mm travel Hummingbird was arguably a little too undergunned for my riding style and preference, the Solstice looked very appetizing. Little did I know that I wouldn’t get to ride one for three years. Earlier this year, that day finally came in the shape of a Neuhaus frame box with a Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork and TRP brakes.

Hailey wrote a phenomenal review of the Hummingbird; I recommend you read it if a 120 mm travel bike is more your style…

Solstice Review Build Logic

When you run a cycling website, you accumulate parts from previous review bikes and purchases over time. That’s definitely the case for me. I move through bikes at a steady cadence, but this year, I reeled back the number of review bikes I took on, hoping to spend more quality time with a few models, rather than run through bikes at my normal frequency.

The Solstice was a bike that demanded some attention with its build kit. I wanted to build a hardtail that embodies my view of a bomber, all-metal build kit.

Nothing More, Nothing Less

Looking at my parts bin, mostly leftover from the Sour Cowboy Cookie, a bike I still dream about, I took the wide and strong Astral Serpentine wheels, wrapped in Schwalbe’s award-winning Radial tires, along with the Ratio Mech, titanium Lucky Riser Doom bars, a 22.2 Paul Boxcar stem, and those killer Cyber Cycles steel cranks. The 220 mm travel dropper post just made the bike look all the more capable. When I sent Daniel Yang an initial build photo, he replied with “Nice! Slick build, massive dropper!”

Long-leggedness aside, I’d quite liked all of the gear leftover from the Sour build and felt like sticking with a mostly familiar build kit could help me isolate what exactly that slender steel frame would be doing under my legs as I lightfootedly pedaled it all over the Santa Fe National Forest.

While this is by no means close to how Neuhaus would spec one of its complete frame offerings, for me, it balances capable but steezy parts that are as good-looking as they are reliable. And increases the shreddy nature of a 130-travel hardtail frame.

Before we get into that, let’s break it down.

Neuhaus Solstice Quick Hits

  • $1,299 frame
  • $1,899 frame and Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork (discounted price; recommended)
  • Made in Taiwan
  • S-XL (XL reviewed here)
  • XL frame weight: 6.7 lbs with the cable clips, seatpost clamp, and rear axle
  • 32 lbs complete as shown for size XL with an all-metal build including steel cranks
  • 65° HTA
  • 130 mm travel
  • 29″ wheels with 2.6″ clearance
  • Quad-butted, heat-treated 4130 Steel

Daniel Yang and Nick Neuhaus collaborated on the Neuhaus Metalworks line, and the Solstice, to me, embodies what I would call the perfect hardtail platform. It’s designed for 130 mm of travel with a geometry that is neither too progressive nor too XC. Neuhaus recommends you build it with big brakes, burly tires, and a stout fork. When combined together, its pleasantly compliant steel chassis creates one of the best riding experiences I’ve had from a Taiwan-made frame.

Rider Profile

I’m a big dude at 6’2″, 210 lbs, with long legs and long arms. In these photos, my saddle height is 83 cm. My riding is exclusive to primitive and technical singletrack. Steep up, steep down, loose, chunky, with a few moments of respite found in some “flowy” sections. In terms of riding style, I like to actively use the trail, hitting different lines each ride and jibbing all the way down. I prefer frames with some flex and usually avoid overly stiff bikes. I live in Santa Fe, New Mexico, at 7200′ in the Rocky Mountains. Most of my riding these days is in the Santa Fe National Forest.

Solstice Geometry

Hell fuckin’ yes, praise to the Necronomicog, someone made a proper ETT for a size XL. Knowing exactly how I like my bikes to fit and sizing them off ETT – sorry, Travis – I was elated to see the Solstice’s size XL come with a whopping 674 mm ETT. Other notes that caused pause were the 65º head angle, another metric perfect for this class of MTB, and a 74.5º seat tube angle, which, for the sake of the Solstice’s designed terrain – the Bay Area – felt modest, without being too progressive. More on that later.

The Doom Lucky Riser bars and a modest 2 cm of spacers under the stem brought the bars close to being level with my saddle, a metric that helps with understanding stack height’s relationship to its rider. I’m still waiting on Spencer’s Dust-Up on that topic! The Solstice has a 150 mm head tube, which is a welcome change from previous size XL bikes I’d ridden with 130 mm head tubes. The top headset cup is external, with the lower headset bearing internal. As a long-legged fella with an 83 cm saddle height and 175 mm cranks, the bike has a certain steeze that is undeniable for a seemingly conservative hardtail package.

Solstice Frame Details

Neuhaus frames lack ostentation. There aren’t details that stand out from the sea of steel hardtails, save for two areas: the chainstay yoke and stand-off seat tube bottle bosses. I’ve long lauded the brand’s eye for proportions. The tubing diameters look neither too slender nor too beefy. The bike can fit two bottles in all sizes, with the larger sizes eking out two large bottles. Thanks to the seat tube bottle mount, you don’t have to worry about your dropper post hitting bottle bosses either.

Chainstay yokes maintain enough clearance for 2.6″ tires and 38-tooth chainrings. The frame is 1x compatible only, as most modern hardtails are; it’s optimized for 1x drivetrains, and the Solstice uses a UDH dropout design. The yoke also provides a nice “sand shelf” to display your recent soil accumulations. Loam, dust, or sand. Your pick!

A beautiful, Tapered IS42/52 head tube omits external cups in favor of hidden bearings, IS brake mounts allow for big rotors with the use of an adapter, and a 73 mm BSA bottom bracket shell keeps it simple. The cable management is nice and tidy with M5 bolt-on cable cradling on the underside of the top and down tube.

It’s an incredibly well-thought-out frame, considering hardtails are one of the simplest off-road phenotypes. In fact, my only request for the Solstice V2 is more seat stay bridge clearance, as with my 2.6″ measured tires, the occasional rock gets picked up and pings against the bridge.

Cotta Frame Flex

Using our Pasta Cook metric for frame flex, I was pleasantly surprised by the Solstice’s flex. Granted, I’m on the size XL with the 674 mm ETT, so it’s a long bike. Sitting on the saddle and swaying hips side to side delivers a comfortable amount of wiggle, but not so much that the bike gets lost underfoot in steep and rocky terrain. It’s the “right” amount of flex for a bike that has no rack mounts, in my opinion. Neuhaus didn’t design it for bike camping; they designed it for comfortable compliance during everyday rides.

I reached out to Nick Neuhaus and asked him what his intent was with the Solstice frame flex:

“We designed each size to have similar ride feel across the size range. Our goal is for every size rider to have the same experience with their bike. A rider on a medium should get the same feeling from their bike that you get from an XL. ”

At the end of the day, I never felt like I was fighting the frame in the chunk or pressing against a stiff chassis. Nor did I feel any noticeable heft while climbing. And while bike weight isn’t a real concern for me, a rider pushing 210 lbs with all his gear on, I would put this frame in line with US-made hardtails I’ve ridden that were designed specifically for my weight and riding style.

Taiwan-made frames often err on the stouter side because the manufacturer designs them for the masses. Yet the Neuhaus pushes in the opposite direction, designing around frame feel and flex and keeping it lean and mean.

Neuhaus Solstice on Climbing

Now, I do believe that bike weight doesn’t matter in a subjective way, but having a light-feeling frame under you while you tackle a 5,000′ climb is objectively an added bonus. With my full-metal build kit, I opted for the Schwalbe Magic Mary and Albert combination I lauded on my Meriwether. This tire combination allows for endless gecko-like grip when scaling our chunderous climbs in the Southern Rockies. While climbing over springtime post-monsoon wet roots, slick rocks, and damp soil, or the dregs of a dry summer where everything was blown out, the Radial tires found purchase and the Solstice’s geometry felt familiar.

Most modern bikes are hovering around a 77º seat tube angle. On a full-suspension bike, you sag into a rear shock and a front fork, but on a hardtail, a static, non-sagged 74.5º seat angle steepens with front-fork sag. Neuhaus lists its geo unsagged, so when the trail got steep and techy, perched on the nose of the saddle, I could dig in over the bottom bracket more to climb efficiently.

Frame design is a part of the whole equation, and as the seat angle steepened, so did the head angle, which made it easy to flick and maneuver the front end when needed as well. The 56 mm of BB drop kept the 175 mm cranks mostly free of pedal strike as well. Long cranks are left out of the conversation in most bike media, and if you haven’t figured out how to ratchet your pedals through techy sections, it’d be a good thing to learn. Pedal strikes are always avoidable.

I’d hate to have the Solstice’s BB go any higher or lower, for that matter, because this bike is a fucking beast on the descents.

Unhinged, Psychotic Descents

Wide bars, supple fork, grippy tires, compliant wheels, and a thousand-yard stare down the trail, and the Solstice, even only having 130 mm of travel, becomes a veritable plow on the descents. On trails I’d normally want to tap on the brakes on similar-travel spec bikes, for some reason I wanted to push my limits harder on the Solstice. Coming right off the Revel Rascal review period, I was nervous I’d be missing the Rascal’s calm and centered demeanor, but by contrast, the Solstice felt inherently scrappy and would roll up its sleeves every time I pointed it downhill.

There isn’t a world where I’d request even the slightest geo tweak with this bike. It hammers on techy trails, and when there’s a trailside booter, like the ones often featured in my bike reviews that are found on my lunch lap, it enjoys being aloft. I hadn’t ridden a hardtail that liked to get aloft since the Viral Derive. And a lot of that has to do with Nick Neuhaus’ background in BMX and dirt jumpers. He likes a higher BB because it makes the bike more flickable, going against the modern parlance of a “long, slack, low” approach to geometry where a lower bottom bracket puts you more “in” the bike; the Solstice feels like you’re riding atop it like a dirt jumper.

Insert Synonym for Confidence-Inspiring Here

A lot of this camaraderie I felt with the Solstice had to do with the parts spec as delivered from Neuhaus. Yes, I supplied the cockpit and drivetrain, but Nick and Daniel from Neuhaus encourage people to use the TRP brakes and Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork. Their reasoning follows my own thoughts around riding Mavens on a hardtail: the more raw power, the better.

High-speed descending requires immediate power for when the line choice goes pear-shaped. I definitely pushed myself riding the Solstice and was always thankful for the bite of the TRP calipers, delivered by the slightest pull of the lever. This acute sensation takes a bit to get used to, and a few corners were undeservingly skidded during our dry summer months before I figured out the bite point-to-traction ratio later on.

Another intended spec is the Fox 36 SL Performance Grip. It’s only got three options for compression: Open, Medium, and Firm, and 17 rebound clicks. Initially, when I had Rusty at the Broken Spoke build up the bike, I’d brought a 36 SL Grip-X fork, thinking I’d want more adjustment and fine-tuning on the Solstice. Much like the Grip-X 34 I’d ridden on the Retrotec, I found that I value Fox’s LSC adjustment for hardtails to ensure proper support.

After the first ride, however, my perspective quickly changed, favoring the simplicity of the Fox 36 SL Performance Grip package. Setting the settings dead center on the rebound and compression in the Open position all the time, I never touched the fork throughout the three-month review period and hundreds of miles of singletrack.

A Parts to the Whole Equation

Yes, powerful brakes and a no-bullshit fork go a long way, as does a familiar-feeling cockpit and drivetrain. It makes it easier to evaluate the bike you’re reviewing, and familiarity makes for a more fulfilling experience. I didn’t have to get used to new tires, or a new drivetrain, or worry about bashing around on some new-to-me wheels. I could focus on what makes the Solstice such a capable and damn fun bike.

Displaying what I believe is the penultimate mountain bike setup – the ultimate being a 120/140 full suspension – my Solstice build achieves a balance of keeping things relatively light while maintaining realistic dependability and durability. All of that works in favor of a frame with just the right amount of wiggle and shimmy.

Riding the Solstice reminded me how much I love hardtails: their simplicity, honesty, and, when done right, capability. I never felt undergunned to the point of checking myself, nor did I wish I’d grabbed a full suspension. A lot of that has to do with how I know the line on every trail in my backyard, so there’s an operator’s efficiency to the equation; but had I ridden unfamiliar terrain, the bike’s familiarity would have helped me just as much, ending my ride unscathed.

Neuhaus got the parts to the whole equation dialed on this frame. The tubing spec, details, and ride feel are dialed. Even the enamel mug blue-inspired paint grew on me! I don’t say this often – and if I do, someone in the comments will undoubtedly correct me – but this is my favorite Taiwan-made steel hardtail I’ve ever ridden.

If it had come in Desert Tan, I might not send it back!

TL;DR

In a mountain bike industry that treats the hardtail as a novelty or beginner’s bike, it’s nice to see brands like Neuhaus Metalworks put their heart and soul into a bike like the Solstice. Equally at home in Marin County or in the rough and rugged Sangre de Cristo Mountains of New Mexico, this bike has the heart to be pushed to the limits, while offering plenty of clearance for big rubber, a burly fork, and powerful brakes. Its chassis flexes in just the right amount, coming in at “Cotta” on our frame flex pasta cook chart.

I’d recommend buying it as a frame with the Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork, since I think it’s a perfect pairing, and then swapping in your parts. Of course, for Neuhaus, they would prefer to sell a complete to you, but if you’re being budget-conscious, I think the frame and fork package price of $1,899 is a fair consideration. Maybe spring for those TRP brakes too if you like instant, immediate power.

Three years ago, I saw a rolling prototype of this bike and fell in love; now, after this review period, my heart is full of admiration for what the team has achieved. I know this all sounds hella cheesy, but I’m being sincere here. The Solstice remains mild-mannered, collected, and cool when it needs to be, but it can also be wielded like a broadsword in the battle of Osgiliath on descents. It’s a simple but capable hardtail; nothing more, nothing less.

Pros

  • Progressive-ish geo
  • Appealing price
  • Flexy (in a good way) frame
  • 130 mm is just enough travel to get rowdy on
  • 2.6″ tire clearance
  • Lightweight at 6.7 lbs for the frame and 32 lbs complete as shown

Cons

  • No sliding dropouts for single-speeders
  • Some might say it’s expensive for a steel frame hardtail
  • Seat stay bridge could use like 5 mm more clearance
  • Geo might not be progressive enough for some riders

Check out more at Neuhaus Metalworks.

The post Neuhaus Metalworks Solstice Hardtail Review: Nothing More, Nothing Less appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Fizik Versor 2 MTB Shoe Review: Trail Tools – John Watson
entry.content:
John’s been wearing the Fizik Versor 2 MTB shoe for a few months in the Southern Rockies, on long days out and trail-work outings. He’s got some thoughts in a quick review…

Shoes, like saddles, grips, and gloves, are a highly subjective product to review. Everyone’s feet are different. Some are bony, skinny, and prone to injury, while others are bigger, wider, and more robust. Mine are the former. Long, skinny, and bony. So when a shoe touts a secure fit with lightweight protection like the Fizik Versor 2, I’m interested. But before we get into that…

Fizik Versor 2 Quick Hits

  • $149.99
  • Size 36 – 48
  • 980 grams for size 47 shown here
  • Black (shown) or white
  • SPD cleat compatible
  • Also available as a flat pedal
  • Vibram sole
  • Ripstop fabric: woven fabric resistant to tearing and ripping
  • Laced closure for the BOA-averse riders

Construction

The Versor 2 features a stretchy sleeve to keep rocks, dirt, and debris out of the shoe. It uses a lace-up closure, rather than Velcro straps or BOA systems common in many modern shoes. The Vibram sole and outsole cover a ripstop woven fabric on the upper, designed to resist abrasion. These are stout, heavy-duty shoes, built for trail riding. Yet my size 47 weighs only 980 grams (2.15 lbs) for the pair, including cleats. I have to install my cleats really far back, and Fizik’s cleat beds always allow for the correct positioning for my bike fit.

Fit and Feel

The first time I laced up the Versor 2, I had to mess a bit with the lace tension. Laces tend to stretch as you ride, particularly on new shoes, so leaving them too tight is better than too loose. For someone who has long, bony feet, the shoes felt super secure and comfy. In fact, they’re the most comfortable off-the-bike shoe I’ve worn in terms of sole support and walking comfort.

Off the Bike: Trail Work

This summer ended with a flood of rain, and with it came a slew of downed trees and washouts in need of repair. All of my rides require some form of trail work these days, with either a packable pocket chainsaw or the big boss of trail saws, the Hunkenr that Travis reviewed. For bigger jobs, I’ll pack in my Trail Boss tools and climb up to the area in need of work.

Not only are the Versor 2 shoes incredibly supportive during this sort of work, but they also grip incredibly well, even after getting wet. Using a McLeod tool or Rogue hoe, flinging dirt and rocks out of the way, the elastic sleeve around the opening kept my shoes free of debris. I never felt the shoes rub up on the heel, which would cause blisters to form during a long day’s work.

The rubber outer and Vibram soles withstood a good amount of abuse while maintaining their tread pattern. Overall, in terms of comfort and durability, I’d give these a high rating, if it weren’t for a single incident I had last month.

On the Bike: Into the Rocks

On a ride with friends in the Sierra, I hucked my Significant Other Ded Rek into a rocky chute, only to be greeted with a giant piece of rock straight to the shin. Luckily, the impact happened under a pair of socks, which the rock cut into, along with my Versor 2 shoes. The little gash on the left foot shown in these photos came from this impact. I’d never, ever cut shoes like that on rocks, having kicked and shinned a number of sharp impacts over the years.

All this to say, I was shocked. The cut went clear through the ripstop and the hard plastic shank of the shoe. Who knows what damage this impact would have done to other shoes I’ve worn over the past few years, and my shin certainly took the brunt of the impact, with a scab that continuously fell victim to other trail abrasions and took forever to heal. But it did cause pause.

These two photos show the interference with the top of my foot and the laces wing at the top of the shoe…

Versor 2 Achilles

As I said in the beginning of this review, shoe reviews are hella subjective. What bothers my feet might not bother yours. But one thing I found was that, in order to have the correct tension with the laces to form a secure, snug fit, the little wing where the top lace loops through dug into my foot. After a big day of climbing, it was noticeably tender, and the following day, the spot would be sore when I put the shoes back on.

What the Versor 2 Gets Right vs. Wrong

Durability, feel, support, and looks are all where the Versor 2 lands a dang near perfect rating. However, the closure system and the hard laces digging into my foot make me question how much longer I’ll want to wear them. But YMMV, and not everyone’s foot profile is the same. Placing that critique aside, I can’t think of a more bomber shoe I’ve owned in recent years, where a shoe is comfortable both on big backcountry days and after a full afternoon of trail work.

Working on trails is a full-body effort, and our feet can withstand a lot of abuse. The Versor 2 nailed both on- and off-bike feel, and this pair has endured a good amount of abuse. Aside from a single tear and a subjective fit issue with the shoe’s silhouette, they’ve been bomber.

Pros

  • Elastic cuff enclosure keeps debris out
  • Vibram sole is hella grippy
  • Exceptionally comfortable in terms of sole support
  • Cleat install is easy, offering plenty of fore/aft adjustment
  • Price ain’t bad. Not cheap. Not expensive.

Cons

  • Fit issues (for me, but perhaps not for you)
  • Durability questions from a single rock strike

See more at Fizik.

The post Fizik Versor 2 MTB Shoe Review: Trail Tools appeared first on The Radavist.
