entry.title: COROS Pace 4 Pro In-Depth Review: Worth the Upsell?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The COROS Pace 4 Pro at first glance might just look like a premium materials Pace 4, and in many ways, there’s a fair bit of truth to that. And there’s nothing wrong with that, as I’ll dive into. It’s unquestionably a more premium watch than either the Pace 4 or Pace Pro, and it’s got a new heart rate sensor too (don’t worry, plenty of accuracy testing below).

But from a company standpoint, it represents a clear attempt at trying to break into the premium market. Less ‘trying to make’, and more ‘trying to get people to buy it’. While COROS continually smashes it out of the park when it comes to budget watches (e.g., the Pace 3 and most recently the Pace 4), it has repeatedly struggled to attract buyers to more premium-priced devices that compete head-to-head on price with Garmin. After all, it’s been 5 years since the last major launch of their top-end flagship COROS Vertix 2 (and no, I don’t count the slight materials refresh in the Vertix 2S as a major new watch, and even that was 2.5 years ago).

With the COROS Pace 4 Pro at $449, COROS is trying to thread the line just enough under Garmin’s premium pricing of the Forerunner 570 (at $549) to entice buyers to forget the FR570’s extra software features, and save the cash for ice cream. The question is, does COROS pull it off?

With that, let’s dive into it!

What’s New:

In some ways, it’s hard to have a ‘What’s New’ section when COROS doesn’t have a prior-generation Pace 3 Pro to compare it to. Instead, this watch is basically a re-imagined COROS Pace Pro, but with the ‘4’ stuck in there to keep marketing life simple. Though, it gains some features the Pace 4 added that the Pace Pro lacked.

There, here’s how it differs from the existing Pace Pro:

– Larger 1.47” AMOLED display from 1.3” AMOLED (biggest COROS screen to date)
– Increased pixels (466x466px vs previous 416x416px)
– Increased brightness to 3,500 nits (Pace 4 was 1,500 nits)
– Ability to add up to 11 data fields per page (from 8 fields on Pace Pro)
– Added new multi-data page field that can cram in 13 data fields
– New 4th Gen optical HR sensor (for COROS watch with it)
– Added sapphire glass display
– Added action button (Pace Pro doesn’t have that, though Pace 4 does)
– Added microphone (Pace Pro doesn’t have that, though Pace 4 does)
– Added voice control from watch (Pace Pro doesn’t have that, though Pace 4 does)
– Added full speaker (neither Pace Pro nor Pace 4 had that)
– Added ability to take calls from watch (neither Pace Pro nor Pace 4 had that)
– Added GPS ‘Auto’ mode (dynamically selects required satellite level)
– Increased maximum GPS battery from 38 hours to 60 hours
– Improved bezel material from plastic to titanium
– Increased weight from 32.5g to 38g
– Doubled the onboard RAM
– Same 22mm band size (same as Pace 3/4, Pace Pro, APEX 2 Pro, APEX 4 42mm)
– Priced at $449USD, 449EUR, $799AUD, 389GBP, 619CAD

From a software standpoint, there are actually no new software features here. At least unique/specific to the Pace 4 Pro. Instead, all the COROS watches are getting their usual roughly quarterly update of software features, and the Pace 4 Pro is part of that (as is the Pace Pro). For example, for September this included an update to the Adventure Journal (mostly on-app), the option to directly transfer firmware via computer, and cycling climb alerts on the watch (previously this was on Dura). Also recently there was a revamped sleep score and sleep metrics on the COROS app.

In terms of color options, there’s black and white, each with either the silicone or nylon straps:

In terms of all the other usual bits for recent COROS watches, it’s got:

– Global offline mapping pre-installed (and free downloadable updates)
– Turn-by-turn navigation with pre-planned route
– Barometric altimeter
– Dual-frequency/multiband GNSS/GPS
– 32GB of Storage
– 447 mAh battery capacity
– 5ATM (50m) water resistance
– Access to the COROS MCP for connecting to Claude & ChatGPT

Next, looking at the size, here’s how things compare:

Also, importantly, the display itself is identical in size to that of an Oreo. Concerned about accuracy, I measured it three times with three different Oreos. I can confirm all three Oreos tasted great. I mean…they were all properly calibrated to match the display.

Finally, from a battery chart standpoint, here’s where things stand:

Just to quickly cover this chart with my real-world testing. When it comes to daily battery life, I’m seeing roughly 4-6 days in the real world (which is inclusive of 1-2 hours of GPS workouts per day).

For the workout claims, I’m simply not getting anywhere near those results. They claim 30 hours in always-on display mode with Max GPS, yet I’m consistently under 20 hours, sometimes low 20 hours. For running, they’re saying it may be a bug with the GPS subsystem. For cycling, it’s also been consistently estimated at 20 hours. In cycling, they say that’s because of a bug in how the device goes into Bluetooth accessory scanning mode each time I stop (including even at stop lights/stop signs), searching again for any sensors it can’t find (such as those for other bikes). As a result, in cycling mode it’s barely achieving an estimated 20 hours of battery life. COROS says they plan an update in November to address this.

With that, let’s dive into the daily basics!

The Basics:

In this section, I’ll cover all the daily basics of using the watch. Things like the hardware, user interface, activity/sleep tracking, and more. Then after that we’ll dive into all the sports bits, following which I’ll cover the accuracy of the new heart rate sensor, as well as GPS accuracy.

Starting off with the hardware aspects, the unit has three buttons, with one of them being the Digital Crown. On the left side you’ve got a button that opens up a quick-access control panel (for enabling/disabling things like sleep mode, or satellite modes, speaker volume, etc.). This was previously the Action Button on other recent watches, but now it is more…ummm…actionable. During activities it switched to the map page.

Meanwhile, on the right side, there’s the Digital Crown for scrolling through menus (and pressing enter to start a workout), as well as the lower right button, which acts as a ‘back/escape’ option.  You can long-hold the lower right button to get to the controls menu.

As for the Digital Crown, as always I like them for scrolling in maps, but otherwise I find them finicky on a sports watch. This includes on Apple Watches just as much as COROS watches. That said, with the touch screen on the COROS watch, I’ll generally use that for getting around menus instead, so it’s mostly a wash here.

Next, the Pace 4 Pro has a much brighter 3,500 nit display – by far the brightest display from COROS. Do keep in mind though, that every company advertises *peak* brightness, not actual constant brightness levels, which are variable based on the ambient light sensor. No company can maintain an AMOLED display at 3,500 nits constantly without slaughtering the battery and display life.

That said, it’s also unnecessary to do so. I live on an island in the Mediterranean, where it’s bright and sunny, and I have no issues seeing the Pace 4 Pro in any lighting conditions (including bright sunny days), and most of the time I can tell it’s clearly not at 3,500 nits (because even 1,500 nit watches are more than enough for sunny days).

Here’s the Pace 4, Pace Pro, and Pace 4 Pro side-by-side in direct sunlight:

In the above case, all units were set to their default brightness settings of ‘Standard’ (there are three levels: Standard/High/Max). Point being, even on the lowest level, I had no issues at all.

Now, one nifty thing here is the new battery usage feature COROS recently added to their app. This lets you see what drives battery level for each function. The problem is, as nifty as this is, it’s also hilariously wrong when it comes to sport usage. I’d argue it’s heavily misleading, though I think that misleading aspect is more engineering geekery than purposeful deceit. The reason is that the % listed next to the activity level is incorrect. Instead, it’s *only* looking at the GPS function specifically, not the processing pieces, which get bundled under ‘General Use’ and ‘Daily Features’, making it seem far higher in GPS time than reality.

So, let’s look at today’s run I just did (90 mins). In this case, looking at the battery chart, it shows a mere 2.6% above.

But in reality, you can see the before/after photos I took, where the battery went from 69% to 61%:

Since the beginning of watch time (including COROS’s own GPS battery claim chart shown above), you’d list this as 8% battery loss. Not 2.6% battery loss. I brought this up to COROS (for a different workout/ride), and it sounds like some changes might be on the way, with them saying:

“Lastly, sorting out the battery health / usage topic with our PM now and we are sorting out a way to display battery drain for an activity with sub-items all from within the activity usage, so in your example you would see 15% as the total activity amount rather than 8% for the activity, and the other 7% placed under other categories.”

Hopefully that’ll happen, as the feature is actually really really cool, and better than anything else out there for sports watches (Apple has some elements of this on the app, and Garmin has most aspects of this on the watch, but COROS implements it better UI-wise long-term in the app).

Nonetheless, moving along, here’s the stock watch face. As with other COROS watches, you can customize plenty of it within the watch itself, or from the COROS app:

Sliding down from there are the widgets. Each widget glance of sorts can be opened up to see more details about it. For example, here’s the daily activity widget showing today’s activity details, and then if I crack that open, I can get those metrics trended over 7 days:

Scrolling down from there, there’s a handful of others as well. I can customize these, including whether they appear, as well as the order:

Of course, one of them is sleep metrics. Here I can see my sleep summary details, as well as my deeper stats like sleep phase/stage time.

All of this is also displayed on the COROS App, including newly revamped sleep pages with sleep score details, and tons more sleep data. Or at least, the presentation of the data is improved.

Additionally, in the event you take a nap, COROS will show nap details. In fact, I really like the way they show your different sleep bits on a single page, and even offer the ability to merge things together. Like, for example, two days ago when I went to bed too late, then we had some bonkers-crazy thunderstorms in the middle of the night that kept all the kids up for a bit. Point being, by the time I got back from school drop-off rounds, I just went back to sleep for 90 minutes.

As for the accuracy of these metrics, I focus specifically on the times I went to sleep and woke up. And these have been mostly spot-on, though, last night wasn’t great. I don’t compare sleep phase/stages, because that’s mostly fake-science for clicks. The accuracy of those metrics from so-called gold-standard methodologies is only about 80% accurate. So trying to compare one device to something that’s at best 80% accurate isn’t super helpful to anyone. Thus, I won’t waste your time with that.

Instead, if we look at last night, for example, here’s how things handled (I was reading on my phone for a while):

Feel Asleep (Actual): ~12:50-12:55AM
COROS Pace 4 Pro: 12:01AM
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 12:50AM
Garmin Cirqa (Bicep): 11:56PM
Whoop 5.0/MG: 12:52AM
Amazfit Helio (Bicep): 12:55AM
Fitbit Air (Bicep): 1:03AM

Woke Up (Actual): Alarm at 7:50AM, snoozed to 7:58AM
COROS Pace 4 Pro: 7:58AM
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 7:58AM
Garmin Cirqa (Bicep): 8:00AM
Whoop 5.0/MG: 7:56AM
Amazfit Helio (Bicep): 7:58AM
Fitbit Air (Bicep): 7:49AM

Next, one of the metrics it’ll capture while you’re sleeping is your overnight HRV. It’ll trend this over time after you’ve established your baseline metrics, showing things like ‘Normal’ or outside of ranges:

Here’s how that compared last night:

COROS Pace 4 Pro: 64ms
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 66ms
Garmin Cirqa (Bicep): 63ms
Whoop 5.0/MG: 63ms
Amazfit Helio (Bicep): 68ms
Fitbit Air (Bicep): 55ms

As you can see, virtually all of them are the same. Save the Fitbit Air, which I find consistently low for whatever reason.

Now, all of these metrics (HRV, sleep, activity, etc.) are pulled into the COROS app on your smartphone, where you can view them and dig into more details for any of them. You can also adjust these tiles as you see fit:

Next, switching topics, at this juncture COROS has yet to implement a real LED flashlight into their watches. Still, they do offer a simplistic screen-based flashlight. And given the brighter 3,500-nit display, it works just fine.

That said, I’m really hoping COROS joins the Flashlight Club (which currently contains Garmin, Suunto, and Amazfit). It’s just more practical to have the flashlight pointed at the thing you’re trying to illuminate, rather than illuminating my own face.

Now when it comes to music, note that the COROS Pace 4 Pro does have music storage on it, but realistically you probably won’t use it. It supports downloading MP3 files, and then pairing up your headphones via Bluetooth. But of course, in 2026 almost nobody is doing that. They’re instead using platforms like Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, etc., which COROS doesn’t support (certainly COROS would love to support those platforms, but those major platforms have largely gatekept their services).

That said, you can control music/media on your phone, such as podcasts or any other platform:

Oh, and lastly, there’s the voice control bits. There’s actually a few different features that leverage the microphone, both in workout mode (like saving voice notes), as well as afterwards for saving workout notes. But in regular mode, you can also use it to simply use your watch to open things. Just long-press the lower left button. For example, you can ask it to start a run:

Now, as I’ve said on countless other watches, I’m not really a ‘talk to my wrist’ guy. And especially not a ‘it takes longer to talk to my wrist and wait than just press the darn button twice’ kinda guy. I’m sure down the road years from now this sort of thing will be faster and more useful, but these days it’s mostly a gimmick to me. Nonetheless, to each their own!

With that, let’s head out for a workout.

Sports Usage:

Next up, if you’re buying a COROS watch, you’re almost certainly doing so for some sort of sports usage. So in this section I’m gonna go through all those pieces, including during workouts, post-workout training load and recovery pieces, as well as a bit of offline mapping and navigation components. To be clear, absolutely nothing here has changed since any other recent COROS watch (which are all running essentially the same software). Instead, the changes around sport usage mainly come from heart rate accuracy, which I cover in the next section.

In any case, the first step is choosing a sport mode. The COROS Pace 4 Pro has virtually all the major sport modes you’d expect. It’s not quite the Girls Gone Wild listing of some 200 sports modes of Amazfit, but it gets the job done. The main ones you’d be missing compared to some of COROS’s higher-end watches are around climbing (e.g., rock climbing). But if heights aren’t your jam, then you won’t miss anything here.

In any case, to select a sport mode, you’ll tap the upper right button and scroll through the sport modes to find your pain:

Once you’ve done that, it’ll go off and find GPS (if outdoors), as well as any sensor accessories (such as cycling power meters or an external heart rate sensor). It’s here that you can select things like structured workouts, basic interval workouts, and apply a route for navigation. Or just tweak other sport settings.

In our case for today’s run, I’m going to load up a route/course. I created this route in Strava, which then pushed to my COROS account. Though (still) annoyingly, COROS doesn’t automatically transfer that to my watch. I’ll need to go into the COROS app and then select to push it to the watch. I know I’ve harped on this for years, but when it comes to tiny features that are actually helpful to athletes, just syncing the darn route is so much more useful than voice prompts.

Once I send it to the watch, it appears here to select, along with some quick stats about the run:

You can also, of course, create routes on other platforms, import GPX files, and create routes within the COROS app as well (including creating waypoints).

Once all that is sorted, out we go for our run. While running, you’ll see the data pages as you’ve configured them. All of this is pretty straightforward:

When it comes to that route, you’ll see your route overlaid atop the map, and then get turn notifications ahead of each turn (about 50m away while running/hiking, a bit further while cycling). It’ll indicate which way to turn:

If you go off-route, then the watch will let you know within about 50m as well. Note that the COROS watches don’t support offline re-routing. It’ll simply let you know which compass direction the actual route is, and it’s up to you to figure that out.

You can also see your elevation profile of the planned route, and other handy stats:

Plus, automatic climb details will engage as you hit a climb:

In the event you want to create a voice note, pinned to the location, for later inclusion in your workout journal, you can do that via the controls menu. These will then show up as notes (with your voice note using the microphone) on the journal and workout track. Again, it’s not really my jam, but I know people who do find the voice notes useful for scouting things. Note the play button below, and then the automatic transcription (I include the actual audio in my review).

Once your workout is complete, you’ll see all the summary stats on the watch, such as this from today’s trail run:

And you can also add yet another voice note, this time for RPE. I’ve skipped that, and just went with smiley-face style. That’s more my jam.

Then, once this all syncs to the COROS app, you can see your full workout details here; note in particular, it’ll show your voice notes on the map itself, and you can also add in photos from the workouts, which will show up accordingly in the right spots using GPS information.

When it comes to training load metrics, COROS has a basic Race Predictor feature, a Running Score feature, and Training Load metrics. Here’s the Race Predictor feature. Note that this really only takes into account flat-ground runs, and not hilly trail runs like mine. In my case, the vast majority of my runs are trail runs (and specifically, very hilly ones), so my numbers rarely get updated here.

There’s also your overall training Intensity and Recovery metrics. I find the recovery metrics reasonably close to how I’m feeling.

Next, there’s training load. And like clockwork, I’m going to complain again that this resets every single Monday. In real life, training load doesn’t reset every Monday. If you did the Berlin Marathon on Sunday, you still very much have that training load in your legs Monday morning (as any staircase will remind you). Yet for COROS, it all disappears. Here’s my Sunday night:

And then the next day it’s zero. Sigh.

I’m hoping if I keep banging this drum, COROS will finally change it. They did on the smartphone app, but not yet on the watches. Eventually?

Heart Rate & GPS Accuracy:

First, let’s look at a lazy interval workout yesterday; you can see that overall it’s mostly good. There’s one minor error early on for a few seconds, then it sorts itself out. Along with some slight delays coming down from intervals towards the end (as I’d start the walk), though neither is a massive deal. Also very, very slight delays on the start of some intervals, but nothing you’d likely notice in real life.

Next, we’ve got a harder interval workout at the track. Now, in this case I had a Polar H10 chest strap with me, though apparently it was on its last battery legs, and created a proper mess of things, as you can see below. Still, as for the COROS itself, it happily agreed with all the other devices on this journey, which is good. And if I sift through the mess below, I don’t see any cases where the COROS Pace 4 Pro is out of line here.

Next, some indoor trainer high-intensity intervals. From a cycling standpoint, these 30-second intervals went from 150w to 590w, and were probably the most visible case of delays with the optical HR sensor. You can see it took quite a while to catch up:

That said, for these sorts of high-intensity intervals, the delay of the HR being a few seconds late isn’t usually something most coaches (or analytics aspects) would look at. That’s because HR itself (your actual heart) is a lagging indicator for effort here. Instead, using pace or power is what actually matters here. And you can see in the second half when I lowered the intensity a bit, it was much faster to catch up.

Meanwhile, on this other trainer ride, which was following a virtual route where things were a bit more civil, the two lines are reasonably close. There are some minor quirks coming down from high-intensity moments, where you see a bit of bobble in the HR. Nothing massive, but something that could use a bit of work. Also note the colors are flipped here, just…sigh…because.

The same goes here with another trainer ride. On the whole it’s pretty darn good (though remember, trainer rides are like the easiest thing ever for optical HR sensors). Still, there are some minor mistakes here that could use some work. This kinda vaguely reminds me of Polar’s HR mini-spike/bobbling-drop issues on most of their recent wristwatches.

And then switching to the opposite end of the spectrum in terms of difficulty for optical HR sensors to track, is an outdoor ride. Here we can see that, on the whole, it’s got the gist of things. But we can also see numerous errors/offsets, especially at higher intensities when things are normally stable. This is actually fairly unusual. Usually for outdoor cycling, once you reach a higher intensity, heart rate readings tend to become easier for devices to track. It’s the transition phase (easy to hard, hard to easy) that most wearables in rougher conditions mess up.

In any case, looking at the new optical HR sensor, I’d argue it is improved over the previous generation, but equally, other companies are also improving. And I’d say those other companies’ pace of improvement is faster than COROS here. Which isn’t to say the above is bad. It’s certainly not. But rather, the bar has been raised, and while COROS has made improvements, their overall place in the standings stays roughly at the upper end of the mid-tier. But it’s far from industry-leading.

Meanwhile, for GPS I’m simply not seeing anything that’s concerning at this point across running (trail running and road running), as well as cycling. For example, a trail run today (in ‘High’, but not ‘Max’), and things are virtually identical to the Fenix 9 Pro:

I’ve got some other watches in this test, but you’ll have to wait till next week for those. Either way, they all match here.

Here’s another trail run, this time versus the Amazfit Dual Solar watch (and Garmin Fenix 9 Pro), at the ‘Auto’ level, all looks well:

Though, you can see in the trails that the COROS Pace 4 Pro easily outperforms the Amazfit unit, which was frequently off in the bushes. I only spend time in the bushes when I need to collect a crashed drone, and this wasn’t one of those times.

Here’s an interval run we did on the streets. Over and over again loops. Loops like this are always fun for repetition purposes on GPS tracks. Again, at a high level it all looks good:

That said, looking closely here, I do see a slight offset by the COROS on this stretch. Again, merely the wrong side of the street, so not a massive deal. Though, consistently the wrong side every loop. The others were correct (we ran down the left side of this deserted street).

Setting aside this street/turn, on the whole I think the COROS Pace 4 Pro has perfectly functional GPS accuracy. As I noted earlier, I remain a bit concerned about the battery burn during GPS workouts, due to bugs COROS says are lingering, causing that battery to be substantially higher than it should be. COROS says fixes are coming in the November timeframe, but as always with GPS vs. battery fixes, there’s usually a tradeoff. Especially in cases like the Auto one where COROS says it’s switching too frequently.

In any case, it’s something I’ll keep an eye out for later this fall.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Wrap-Up:

Overall, the COROS Pace 4 Pro definitely *feels* more premium. It was easily mistaken by friends as a Garmin Forerunner 570 or Forerunner 970 on my wrist numerous times. It looks a lot like it. The display is brilliant, in terms of size and clarity, as well as brightness. Likewise, the titanium bezel looks nice. All of that is good. Whether or not consumers find the $150 upsell over the existing COROS Pace Pro to be worthwhile is probably the bigger question.

COROS has argued in media presentations that it competes with the Forerunner 970. As I noted in the video, that’s simply a hard no. Not even close. On the hardware front, it lacks many of the hardware features the Forerunner 970 has (e.g., the flashlight, medically certified ECG, a much better optical HR sensor, better GPS accuracy, and more). And then on the software side, it’s not even close, no matter which software category you choose. Garmin dominates there (very deeply).

However, compared to the Forerunner 570? That’s fresh meat for the taking. Priced $100 more at $549, the Forerunner 570 lacks offline maps, lacks a flashlight, and lacks ECG. Yes, the Forerunner 570 is an excellent sports/running watch if you exclude those features, and is deeper in most (all?) of the non-mapping sports categories than COROS is. But it’s a price tradeoff that it seems many people are willing to take. COROS is better served to focus on that battle.

But whether those same consumers are willing to pay substantially more than the Pace 4 or Pace Pro for nearly the same software? Now that’s a bigger COROS-focused question that only time will tell. History has spoken loud and clear (repeatedly) that COROS is most deadly when they focus on budget. Though, this time it does somehow feel slightly different.

Either way, I think it’s a great-looking watch that’s coming from a company that continues to push new features to both the app and hardware roughly every quarter, and also continues to add polish to the app & watch firmware.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Huge Amazon Prime Big Deals Sports Tech Tracker!
entry.content:
Amazon’s running its Prime Big Deal Days today and tomorrow (6th and 7th), which includes a decent chunk of sports tech deals – including on some newly released products (like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, Pixel Watch 5, GoPro Mission 1 Pro, and more!).

Here’s the Top 5 items that DC Rainmaker readers bought on Day 1 (and all are still available):

1) Wahoo Fitness KICKR CORE 2 with Zwift Cog V2: This is probably one of the strongest deals, at just $399, including the new Zwift Cog V2 & new Zwift Clicks. Plus, of course, the newish KICKR CORE 2 trainer. There’s also the mechanical 12-spd cassette version too for the same price.

2) Apple AirPods Pro 3 (with optical HR for workouts): Down to just $179, these are both my wife’s and my go-to headphones for virtually everything. Travel, editing, work, workouts, etc…

3) DJI NEO Self-Following Drone: At merely $139USD, this is a steal for one of the best and most indestructible options on the market. Both my kids and I have tried to kill it. No luck. Hundreds of crashes later during all sorts of running, cycling, etc… and it’s still perfectly fine.

4) Anker 25,000mAh Laptop/etc High Speed Power Bank: No surprise, at ~30%, this is a great unit that has become the mainstay of both daily usage (working from a cafe table without a power outlet), to travel usage, to backcountry hikes and long gravel rides. Love it.

5) Garmin Fenix 8 for $731: Again, zero surprise here. Especially with Garmin announcing that almost every Fenix 9 feature is soon coming to the Fenix 8 series, this is a very strong deal.

To take advantage of Amazon Prime Deals, you simply need to be an Amazon Prime member. The good news is that you can sign-up for the free trial and cancel later if you don’t find value in it. Just hit up this giant banner below to do so:

I’ve organized all the best sports technology Amazon Prime Deals (and a few others I’ve found) below in the tables by category. I’ll be updating them throughout the next two days. Keep in mind that not all deals last (in fact, most don’t). So, if you see something that’s hot, I’d strongly suggest buy now (and return later if need be).

With that, onto the deals! And thanks for supporting the site via the links below. As an Amazon Associate, I earn from qualifying purchases. Enjoy!

Watches & Wearables:

This covers anything you can wear that’s watch-like or activity band-like, including sensors.  Generally speaking, you’ll mostly find deals here that are on things I’ve written about in the past.  So you won’t find a deal on some random non-sports tech watch here, or on socks. Unless the socks have some crazy sensor or something in them.

There are no deals currently.

Cycling Gear & Trainers:

Got a bike? Then this section is for you.  Everything from bike computers to bike lights to trainers, it’s all here.  I won’t generally be adding things like brake cables or bike seats here, but if I find a good deal on a cassette to stack on that new direct-drive trainer you just bought, I’ll probably list it here.

There are no deals currently.

And then here’s a separate bucket for trainers and indoor bikes:

ProductSale PriceAmazonSale Notes
Lasko High Velocity Pro-Performance Fan - 15% off$54AmazonThis is one of the most popular indoor trainer fan companies out there, which rivals the Wahoo Headwind fan but cost a fraction of the price. Of course, it lacks ANT+/Bluetooth integration, but realistically if you really want that you can add a smart outlet for $10 to toggle it on/off from your phone if need be. It's one of the ones in my rotation.

Action Cameras & Drones:

Wanna record it?  No better way than an action camera.  Anything that’s action camera-related or drone-related, you’ll find here.  That’s especially true of action camera mounts, which are often found for great deals around the holidays.  Same goes with drones and drone accessories.  Usually a great time to pick up an extra battery or extra props.

There are no deals currently.

Other Sports & Fitness:

Anything else that’s sports and fitness-related that I think is interesting will be here.  It may not be super techy – but it’s stuff that most readers will be using in pursuit of their running/cycling/swimming/hiking/whatever.

There are no deals currently.

DCR Random Gadget List:

These are basically the mostly totally unrelated gadgets and things I think are cool deals that I’ve likely bought one or five of (you can never have too many, right)?  Some of it’s probably photography stuff.  Some of it’s random stuff like chargers and battery packs that I use daily, fun camera gear I use to make videos, like sliders and turntables, and well…just random things you’ll find around the DCR Cave.  It’s all random…but it’s all awesome randomness!

There are no deals currently.

Europe Folks Note: I’ve tried in the past to keep track of all the separate Amazon European sites, and honestly, I have given up. With 100+ products on the US list, and then cross-checking each one manually across each country…has proven impossible. That said, you can click any link and, in theory (strong “hopefully” theory), it’s often also on sale in the EU sites.

With that – thanks for reading, and for supporting the site via the links above.

entry.title: Stages SB200 Indoor Smartbike In-Depth Review: Redemption?
entry.content:
Stages is back. Though they’ve actually been back for a year or so now. But more specifically, they’ve just launched the new SB200 indoor smart bike, which has many ties to the older Stages SB20 launched in 2020, but in reality looks nothing like it.

Now I’ll dive into some of the company bits below (see the section titled ‘Quick Company Update’), but the new SB200 follows much of the indoor cycling trend of focusing on a streamlined design, greater rider fit aspects (e.g., serving both a small rider and a taller rider on the same frame), as well as better handlebar button integration with 3rd party apps. It’s a pattern we’ve seen implemented on full smart bikes from the likes of Wahoo, Technogym, and Wattbike, as well as trainer-mounted smart bike-like frames from Zwift, Elite, and others.

In this case, both me (tall) and my wife (vertically challenged) have been riding the SB200 for all our recent indoor cycling rides. Albeit, admittedly, the bike is technically outdoors. But we won’t let that get in the way of the indoor trend. So I’ve got a pretty good idea of what works well, and what I’m not in love with.

With that, let’s dive right into the newness!

What’s New:

While the SB200 is certainly an evolution of the existing SB20, I’d argue for the most part that’s really only in name. Almost everything else is different. One thing to remember, though, is that when it comes to making indoor bikes, Stages has made far more indoor bikes than literally everyone except perhaps Peloton. And even there, Stages is literally making the newest Peloton commercial bike (you’ll notice it looks a heck of a lot like Stages existing commercial bikes). So…yeah.

However, one of the ‘complaints’ about the previous SB20 was that it felt too much like a gym bike, and less like a bike that would fit in your living room (or garage). And indeed, the thing was a tank. Sure, it could last forever, but equally, it was overkill to the extreme for home usage. Like driving a tank to school.

So, here’s how it’s different:

– Added side-to-side pivoting/movement within the frame (about 2°, adjustable)
– Reduced the weight by 55 pounds/25kg (compared to SB20)
– Added roller wheels at the back of the frame for moving/relocating around the house
– Increased flywheel inertia 5x compared to Stages SB20
– Switched to dual-stage belt drive (versus 1x belt drive on previous unit)
– Adds front LCD/display, showing in-ride stats
– Adds a slate of customizable buttons, also preconfigured for Zwift, Rouvy, TrainingPeaks Virtual
– Adds 5 custom shift/bike profiles, selectable right from display
– Added full shifters, customizable to either SRAM or Shimano-style shifting (previously was just buttons)
– Has braking for in-game usage, as well as just adjusting resistance
– Added WiFi support (including connectivity across trainer control “standards”)
– Added 10hz Race Mode over WiFi (data 10x a second)
– Added 4hz Race Mode over Bluetooth (data 4x a second)
– Added heart rate monitor/sensor bridging (into WiFi/etc)
– Added fully internally-routed wiring to all components
– All hidden-cable wiring, no exposed wires/cabling
– First indoor bike to support OpenBikeControl
– Also supports Bluetooth (including FTMS), Zwift Protocol (No ANT+, though)
– Optional swappable seat post accessory
– Tool for adjusting now built into frame
– Changed from previous bear claw crankset design to different adjustable crank arm design (previous design was susceptible to failure when overtorqued, or sweat pooled in holes driving corrosion faster)
– Changed to measuring power at the brake, versus previous dual-pod crankset design
– Claimed power accuracy of +/- 1%
– Supports both spin-down calibration and manual calibration
– Added built-in spring-loaded phone holder above LCD
– Added secondary tablet holder option
– Added free Stages app that includes craptons of structured workouts for free
– Added support for syncing in TrainingPeaks workouts to app
– USB-C charging ports built-in (2 AMPS)
– Added a simple on/off switch to rear of bike
– Price is $2399USD/ £2199/ €2399

For context, the previous SB20 retailed initially at $2,899, though, like all bikes, it shifted in price over time, especially in/out of COVID. Either way, the SB200 being at $2,399 is quite competitive in the full smart bike realm. Obviously, trainer+frame bikes (like the Zwift Ride) tend to be cheaper, though they also tend to offer less fit adjustability than dedicated smart bikes. There are, of course, other pros/cons to weigh as always. For reference, the KICKR BIKE PRO is at $3,999

Finally, as for general specs (rather than the newness above), here’s the quick and dirty of the core indoor bike specs:

– Internal dual-stage belt drive
– Resistance system: Single coil electromagnetic braking
– Power support to 2,500w (1,500w @ 120RPM, 400w @ 40RPM)
– 2.23” display (128 x 32 dot matrix)
– 40cm handlebar with 31.8mm standard tube
– Handlebar customizable buttons (10 total)
– Handlebar braking and shifting (normal bike style)
– Audible feedback when reaching the end of the cassette/shifting
– Free Stages app for control, customization/setup, structured workouts
– Control over Bluetooth Power, Bluetooth FTMS, OpenBikeControl, WiFi
– 4 concurrent Bluetooth Connections
– 2xUSB-C power (5V @2.0A)
– Q-Factor: 153mm
– Rider range: 147cm to 208cm (4’10” to 6’10”)
– Steel frame, phosphate plating with powder coat
– Bike weight: 70lbs/32.3kg
– Bike length: Min is 127cm (49.9”), max is 137.3cm (54.0”), plus tablet holder is 10cm (3.9”).
– Bike Width: 80.4cm (31.6”)
– Bike Height: From 97.9cm (38.5″) to 117.2cm (46″) (+ tablet holder is 14.8cm)
– Maximum rider weight: 300lbs/136kg

With that, let’s just briefly touch on the company aspects.

Quick Company Update:

One can’t talk about Stages without at least talking about Stages going under. Which they did back in 2024. Like many cycling companies coming out of COVID, they over-invested in inventory, which simply sat around for a market that didn’t materialize.

However, unlike some of the other brands that made this mistake and then went under forever, Stages only temporarily disappeared. Later that year, Giant acquired what was left. Keeping in mind that Giant previously built Stages bikes, and was one of the biggest companies left holding the empty bag.

One could probably argue that in some scenarios, Giant would have done the acquisition prior to bankruptcy, but I’m sure lawyers decided this method was better. Either way, Giant ended up acquiring Stages, and much of the top engineering that was at Stages ended up at Giant. For example, all the same product leads that I knew at Stages for the past 15 years are still there.

Of course, in the short term, none of this made existing Stages customers super happy. There was unquestionably a time period where Stages customers were the ones that got shortchanged here. No service, no parts, no nothing.

However, despite no legal requirement to do so, Stages has gone back and manufactured parts for the previous SB20 (you can find them all here). They’ve opened up support lines for it, and they touted that the current average customer support time is under 4 hours, and the average ticket closure time is under 48 hours. They wholeheartedly agree the customer support situation (meaning, no real situation) a few years ago sucked, but equally they note that if you have an existing SB20 and haven’t tried support in a few years, you should give it a whirl.

Looking at some of the Stages SB20 Facebook owner groups, people generally seem pretty darn happy with the current support situation. Obviously, there are some folks that were wronged years ago, and are still holding that grudge (rightfully or otherwise). But it seems like the situation today isn’t really any different than calling Wahoo, Elite, or otherwise.

Plus, it’s pretty darn unlikely that Giant’s going to disappear anytime soon. Should that happen, we’d have a whole lot of other much bigger problems in the bike industry.

Anyway, take those tidbits for what you want.

Unboxing & Setup:

Man, what a difference this bike is. I remember so clearly getting the Stages SB200 bike all unboxed and set up 6 years ago. It was just so…overly everything. An overly built bike, overly packaged for apparently being dropped out of an airplane at cruise altitude, and an overly long, cumbersome process to get set up. Not hard, not difficult, just a general pain in the butt.

This time though? A world of difference.

The total packaged weight dropped from 160lbs/72.5kg to 103lbs/46.7kg. And the bike itself dropped from 126lbs/57kg to 71lbs/32.3kg. And more than that, Stages has clearly followed in the footsteps of Zwift’s consumer-first assembly aspects.

While it always takes me longer to do unboxing and setup compared to a regular person since I’m filming/photographing it, it’s probably balanced out by me having done so many of them. This one though, was just simply fast, even despite the camera work. After removing the cardboard, you’re left with these pieces:

Above you’ve got:

1. Main frame portion
2. Seatpost + saddle
3. Handlebar
4. Front assembly (that holds the handlebar)
5. Rear base
6. Some power cabling stuff
7. Extra set of feet
8. The tools to assemble it all

You’ll start by attaching the base to the frame, which is just two bolts. Quick and easy.

Side note: on this 2nd step, it has you finger-tighten the bolt. However, in the almost-last-step, you’ll crank that bolt down nice and snug with a tool. If, however, you forget this last step, your bike will soon squeak like an adult movie. I mean, just letting you know from a friend.

Next up, you’ll insert the front handlebar holding assembly, and with it, the wires. This is where I want to point out how clean this setup becomes, with all the wiring internal. You can then see the cover I’ll place over it.

There was just so many little details while I was building it up, that were like “Oh wow, that’s super clever engineering”.

Up top, you’ll do the same thing. You’ll simply connect the two wires together. This is a 4-8 second task. And then the wires are now hidden from view. After that, you’ll install the standard handlebar (which you can swap out), and then snap on/screw-in the cover.

What’s cool here is that hidden under that small circle is a mount for your Garmin or Wahoo unit (or anything else that uses those two mounting types…which is everyone).

At this point, the last piece to do is simply sticking in your pedals and plugging it in. I’ll cover crank arm adjustability bits in the next section.

Again, my entire assembly video file I had recording the entire time is about 25 minutes, and that includes taking a slate of extra photos as I assembled, taking extra close-up video of parts, repositioning a few cameras/things, etc… I bet someone not doing that could probably assemble it all in 15-18 minutes tops. And all of it was silly easy.

Bike Fit Bits:

Next up, let’s talk about adjustability of the bike. As with all indoor bikes, one of the key reasons you choose an indoor bike over your regular bike + trainer, is for multi-person adjustability. Obviously, not everyone is sharing a bike, but it’s a main driver for many people getting such a bike. Starting off with the main adjustable specs, you’ve got:

Rider Height Range: 147cm to 208cm (4’10” to 6’10”)
HB Stack Range: 53.5cm to 72.8cm (21.1” to 28.7″)
HB Reach Range: 34.1cm to 56cm (13.4” to 22.0”)
Crank Length Adjustability: 165mm/170mm/172.5mm/175mm
Rider Weight Allowance: Up to 136kg/300lbs

So let’s go through some of these different areas, starting off with the crank length adjustability. This area has been redesigned, specifically to address issues with the previous bearclaw-style crank arms snapping (mainly when they were over-torqued, and then combined with sweat pooling in the other holes and speeding up corrosion). This new system has two small plates that you match together to pick one of the supported crank lengths above:

It’s a perfectly functional system, though I still kinda prefer the bear claw design. But that’s more due to personal preferences than anything else (and probably a touch that when I test things, having a single piece of crank arm metal means I can usually get power meters torqued on more properly). But again, from a normal user standpoint, this is perfectly functional.

Next, there’s the front-end adjustability. There are two core pieces here. First is the up/down piece of the front handlebars, and then the second is the forward/back piece of those same handlebars.

To adjust the up/down pieces, there’s a bolt down on the fork near the Stages logo; simply rotate that, and up/down you go:

Note that you’ve got this nifty wrench that’s just hanging out in the back seat-stay area, always ready:

Next, there’s the forward/back piece of the entire handlebar assembly (including the phone and/or tablet holder you have there). You’ll adjust the bolt under the front portion of the assembly to tweak this:

And then off you go to wherever you want. Super simple.

While having a hand-clamp like you’d find on the Wahoo KICKR Bike SHIFT/PRO might seem appealing at first glance, the reality is it’s not long-term. The KICKR Bike has long suffered from seatposts that slide, and the front-end adjustably can also be finicky. So as much as I prefer a tool-less design, having a tool that simply has a home in the frame means it takes mere seconds, and the seatpost/front-end/etc. just doesn’t move. Thus, ultimately, it’s a better solution.

In any case, for both myself (6’2/188cm) and my wife (5’2/158cm), we had no problems moving back and forth between us. Once you write down those preferred measurements, then it’s easy to do.

I will say that one gap here is a lack of a simple fit sizing chart, which Zwift provides as a starting point for getting the right sizing. I had attempted to measure my wife’s bike and align it all up, but sometimes getting those things to match can be tricky at best. Same goes for trying to match bike-fit coordinates (especially if those fit coordinates are more for a triathlon bike than a road bike).

Again, there’s obvious benefit to getting a proper bike fit, but the simple reality is that most people aren’t doing that for their indoor bike (or perhaps at all). And thus having a company give a rough estimate of a starting point is really handy.

In any case, finally, there’s adjustability of the saddle itself. While this follows the industry-standard bike seat/saddle rails, it doesn’t follow a normal seat post adjusting system (which uses hex wrenches). Instead, it uses these bolts, which suck for adjusting. I’m just gonna say that straight up, they’re annoying to rotate without hitting the rest of the assembly.

Setting that aside, the other gap here is adjustability of the seatpost fore-aft. By default, you can’t do that. That’s somewhat ironic because Zwift literally just came out with the Zwift Ride V2 addressing this complaint. Of course, Stages has a *TON* of experience in gyms with seatpost adjustability, and their previous SB20 had seatpost fore-aft adjustability.

As a stopgap, you can go ahead and purchase an accessory seatpost that does allow for fore-aft adjustability. But that’s an extra cost. In any case, neither my wife nor I felt it was a deal-breaker, but equally, I do feel like so many other bikes include it by default, and I was kinda surprised this didn’t.

Nonetheless, we had no issues quickly moving it between our different positions. Neither of us has perfected the bike fit numbers yet on this specific frame, probably because both of us can pretty easily ride on any frame roughly in our range without an issue (at least for ride durations up to a few hours at a time).

Daily Usage:


(Yes, sunglasses are sometimes needed here, as this is technically outside, just under a cover)

In this section I want to dive into some of the day-to-day usage bits, including aspects around the handlebars/shifting/etc. First though, I’ll start with the ride feel.

The new SB200 now includes a two-stage belt drive system (compared to one stage previously). Stages says this new system gives them 5x the inertia of the previous SB20. While I don’t have an SB20 handy anymore, I can say the inertial feeling here is very very very smooth. It accelerates well, and I’m quite happy with that. For fun, here’s what it looks like inside:

I’ve actually got to take it apart later today (more details on that in the accuracy section), so I’ll take some of my own shots and update here.

The only downside, though, to the SB200 system is the freehub sound when coasting. While certain outdoor bikes (within the freehub) have that high-pitched clicking sound when you coast down a hill, most indoor bikes don’t. Mainly because nobody actually wants to hear that inside. Yet, the SB200 does, and it’s rather loud when coasting. You can hear this in the video at the start of the post.

This isn’t a deal breaker by any means, but equally, I just kinda wish it wasn’t there. Apparently, you can mitigate this a bit by packing some more grease into the freehub, which reduces the sound notably; though it’s not something I’ve attempted yet. To be honest, this is really the only hardware-specific complaint I have about the SB200.

Otherwise, it’s very quiet, like most indoor bikes these days – essentially quieter than the fan you might have running.

So then, since I already covered adjustability in the previous section, let’s talk about the handlebars here. The new handlebars include proper shifters (the SB20 had lame buttons), as well as braking (which the SB20 did have). But the star of the show is arguably the small display here. I know some people don’t care about displays (and most manufacturers dislike them due to added cost and complexity), but it’s just such a simple practical thing:

This is less so about seeing your power in real time (since whatever app you have likely already does that), but actually useful for selecting your gear configuration. That’s because the SB200 supports up to 5 custom profiles, with different gearing arrangements for each one. That could be two for me and three for my wife. Or it could be five different bikes for me (e.g., road 2x SRAM configuration, gravel/MTB Shimano 1x configuration, etc.). The world is your oyster here, and you can create these in the Stages App. You can see these profiles named on the left page here (along with the ‘Shift Beeps’ setting when you reach the end of range), as well as the options to the right.

Then when you power on the bike, it asks which profile to use, and you simply use the buttons to iterate through them. Brilliantly simple, yet super useful – especially for more than one person sharing a bike.

Otherwise, while riding, it shows your stats. Though I do wish there was more customization here for the data pages/fields. There are a handful to choose from, but I kinda want them to channel their inner Stages Dash bike computer data field geekery. After all, why hold back? It’s just a software list of data fields. Go wild.

In any case, above that is the phone holder, which both my wife and I have really appreciated. Again, simple things, like a simple place to stick your phone (she often reads on her longer trainer workouts). Or the Zwift/etc. Companion app. Love it.

The two posts to the left/right are spring-loaded arms that keep it in place, either vertical or horizontal. The only minor nitpicking I have with it is that when I place my phone horizontally (landscape mode), it’s got a smidge too much force and actually pushes the phone buttons. You can find some slightly off-center placement that manages not to do it, but…it’s not quite perfect.

Of course, the box also includes a full tablet holder. I didn’t use it, simply because my wife and I were mostly using my laptop on my cheap projector stand:

I’m not sure how exactly it came to be that I went from like 5-7 trainer desks to zero trainer desks and a $28 projector stand. But here I am. Ultimately, I suppose space was the main thing for me with my current setup for us.

Oh, and below that phone holder are two USB-C ports:

Next up, the handlebars: I’m totally good with the stock grip tape here, and of course, being 31.8mm standard, you can swap things out if you want.

Meanwhile, the biggest change aside from the LCD is, of course, the full shifters, which feel just like real-world bike shifters. They click nicely, though there’s no drivetrain pulse/vibration like you get on some bikes (such as the KICKR Bike) confirming a shift. But given the tiny display there, it’s not a big deal.

There are also brakes, which will do exactly what the name brakes implies. This is mainly handy for quieting the bike when it’s coasting if you stop pedaling (obviously doing this mid-Zwift ride, though, will stop your avatar…so…beware).

Meanwhile, on the side of the handlebars are the customizable buttons. Five per side, and they are designed to roughly mimic those of the Zwift buttons – and they match directly up to that.

You can customize these within the Stages app, and on a per-app basis (e.g., Zwift, Rouvy, etc.).

From a shifting/etc. standpoint, I’m pretty happy. All things handlebar are good for me.

The last area to mention is movement, as well as sprinting. The SB200 includes feet that compress slightly and allow the entire frame to tilt side-to-side up to 2 degrees (officially). These are similar to numerous other trainers/bikes we’ve seen adopt this in recent years:

In reality, it’ll be more than that, especially if you have a trainer mat there, since that compresses too, allowing (far) more movement, as seen below. But at no point did it feel like it was going to tip over. The back base area is pretty stable there.

Again, the main point of side-to-side tilt/sway is so that it feels like a bit more movement, like on your real bike outside. If a bike has zero movement (e.g., the Tacx NEO Bike), it’s like riding a concrete wall. It just doesn’t ‘give’ and feels unnatural. So, the movement is good here.

Meanwhile, the one downside to the front end being rather skinny and lightweight is that it’s kinda easy to throw it around on a sprint, and it tends to bump up/down a bit on hard sprints. Now as always with sprinting, there’s a portion of the population that believes sprinting is best accomplished by relocating your indoor bike halfway across the living room with exaggerated motions. The other portion simply puts out the power, without the relocation. If you fall into the first category, this bike might not be for you.

In my case, I found that frequent hard sprinting would actually end up shifting the bike forward, causing my cheap $29 Amazon trainer mat to bunch up a bit. You can see it occasionally in the video. I’ve had Amazon mats for years and never quite had this issue; thus, while one might blame it on the cheaper aspect (or perhaps because the legs spread out a bit wider than mine), I think it’s mostly because the whole bike bounces a bit.

One thing that might help here is the RigidRide front fork accessory that Stages is offering, which is mostly meant to cut off the side-to-side front movement. But perhaps that’d also make the front a bit more stable. Nonetheless, this isn’t really an issue that I personally think is a big deal, but just throwing it out there for those that might be more ‘agile’ or ‘robust’ in their sprinting performance.

With that, I think I’ve covered all of my daily riding thoughts, so let’s get into some of the app compatibility bits.

App Compatibility:

The new Stages SB200 bike is very unique in one aspect: It’s the first piece of hardware to support the new OpenBikeControl protocol, which is an emerging standard that gives apps and hardware makers a single open standard again. Previously, that was ANT+ FE-C, then Bluetooth FTMS. But these days, with Zwift and their Zwift Protocol, the openness in the indoor cycling industry (or the entire cycling industry for that matter) is falling apart. Of course, this is mostly due to Zwift and their pushing the Zwift Protocol (which drives trainer/bike companies to support it), but ultimately these same companies are kinda part of the problem, due to them being unable to formally agree on anything.

In any event, the OpenBikeControl protocol is a great first step, and seeing an actual hardware company support it is huge. On the software side, it’s already supported by TrainingPeaks Virtual, MyWhoosh, and a number of smaller apps. I’d love to see Elite, Tacx, and Wahoo make quick work of supporting it. Whether or not Zwift will convince them otherwise remains to be seen.

As a reminder, the main reason OpenBikeControl is interesting isn’t for clean/simple power and trainer control, but rather all the other things that indoor trainer/bike companies want to do around buttons, power validation, etc. Basically, stuff that today they add extra special sauce to make happen (like Zwift does with the Zwift Clicks/Play/Handlebars).

In any case, as for the Stages SB200, it supports the other protocols you’d expect to see today. The only notable exception is not having ANT+ support.  But given the discontinuation of ANT+ nearly two years ago. I don’t think that’s really an issue here, though. Here’s what it does support:

– Bluetooth Power (clean)
– Bluetooth FTMS
– Zwift Protocol (BT/WiFi)
– Open Bike Control (BT/WiFi)
– WiFi: Power meter & trainer control

In addition, it also supports heart rate bridging. This helps save you a channel on Apple TV… Though given the WiFi/etc. aspects, that’s really becoming an issue of the past. You can pair any Bluetooth heart rate monitor to it, and it’ll funnel it in over Bluetooth/WiFi/etc., as a single channel along with the rest of the SB200 data/control.

In my case, I used it with a number of the big apps today without any issues. This included Zwift (all these screenshots are from my rides on the SB200) in both SIM & ERG mode:

As with all the apps in simulation (SIM) mode, it showed gearing without issue, as you can see below (Gear 2-10):

I used it in TrainerRoad in structured workout (ERG) mode:

I used it with TrainingPeaks Virtual in both ERG mode and Simulation mode:

And I used it with Rouvy in simulation mode:

I had no issues pairing it with any of them, nor any issues with shifting/braking/etc. Everything there worked perfectly fine.

Power Accuracy:

As it seems with so many other trainer or indoor bike reviews, things got off to a slightly rocky start here, with the unit not quite being spot-on. Nothing horrendous, but about 5-8w too high in the most common ranges for me (200-350w). Slightly higher above that, slightly lower below that.

I’ll save you tons of extra data sets, but after a lot of throwaway rides, it became clear issue was that when my unit originally left the Stages factory for me some 1.5 months ago, the calibration rig wasn’t yet final. Long story short, Stages was actually able to send over an updated inertia value, based on the inertial data from within the app paired to my bike (it’s kinda neat; it gets a QR code that the app can read and download). Notably, Stages did not actually have any of my comparison data sets at this time, just my note saying things seemed off.

In any event, once I got that value, then doing a short warm-up, followed by a zero offset, and then a calibration (plus a new/final firmware update), the unit was finally sticking the landing. So, let’s look at those numbers.

Note that in this case all data is compared to a set of Favero Assioma Pro RL power meter pedals (dual-sided). I usually like to compare against multiple sets of power meter pedals, but frankly, I spent so much time chasing down offset issues that I didn’t really have the desire/time to deal with some other power meter pedals being a PITA.

We’ll start with a SIM ride first (meaning, just following the virtual gradient, not a structured workout). This ride was done in TrainingPeaks Virtual; here’s that data set:

Above you can see the workout structure, which was a bunch of 590w intervals. Ignore the 4th interval in the second set; I had briefly stopped during the recovery period prior for a few seconds to it to grab a towel slightly out of reach, and TrainingPeaks Virtual had disengaged ERG mode but I didn’t realize it (since the power was so low that my easy pedaling felt basically the same). Once the interval started, there was no viable way to spin up to 590w in that short time period with all the shifting required. Anyway, point being, that was me.

Otherwise though, looking at the above, things look pretty much the same at a high level.

So, picking one of the intervals below, you can see that the power between the two units is quite close. I have no concerns there at this point. Though, you can see there’s quite a bit of variability in the power levels being held. While the jump from 150w to 590 was properly efficient (2-4 seconds), it did overshoot a fair bit initially, then undershot, and then wobbled a bit.

Part of that is due to the flywheel’s inertia. Generally speaking, more inertia makes for a smoother ride (and it does), but it also tends to make it trickier for ERG mode to stick the landings, or be super stable.

In talking to Stages about this (from looking at all my other ERG mode sessions), they noted that different folks prefer different levels of smoothing. I’ve often talked about this in my reviews, and can certainly concede that I generally don’t want much smoothing applied to my ERG workouts. But to me, this just seems too volatile (my wife very much dislikes it).

As a result of my feedback and other reviewers, Stages is going to be introducing a three-toggle system to allow a bit more smoothing to find some middle ground there.

In any case, back to the power accuracy here. Looking at the mean-max graph for this, it’s very close, easily within 1.5% of the pedals (which are measuring upstream, and thus should be slightly higher than the bike drivetrain):

And then likewise, here’s the cadence graph. The cadence on the Faveros appears to be ever-so-slightly smoothed more than the Stages, where the Stages floats about 1RPM up/down most of the workout. You don’t notice it when looking at a single unit by itself (either unit). Only on a chart like this. Either way, not an issue.

Above, the discoloration around the 36-minute marker is when I tried to manually ramp up for that interval I missed, but obviously failed to react fast enough to make it work.

Next, let’s look at a Zwift SIM-mode workout. This one includes a few sprints in there, plus some sustained power bits. Here’s that data:

Again, at a high level, this looks pretty close, but let’s zoom in on some sections. Below we have two different things. First is a bit of a 550-600w surge for about 20-22 seconds. In this case, the two units stay basically spot-on to each other. As you can see, highlighted below, they are within 1% of each other during this.

However, in the second peak above, upwards of about 800w, we see the two units virtually identical for the initial 2-3 seconds (again, within 1%), but then we see the Stages SB200 go a bit higher, roughly 100w higher. Obviously, with just two power meters, it’s hard to know which one is correct for these sorts of sprints. That’s one of the downsides of testing indoor smart bikes.

Two units matching can mean it’s correct, or could frankly mean both are wrong. In this very specific case, I’d edge more towards Favero being correct, given the way the power surges after the initial sprint portion (since most of my sprints tend to reach their highest power initially, and then taper off).

In any case, a bit later, two dual sprints in the 800w-900w range, and while the timing is about 1-second difference on these (welcome to the world of 1-second recording rates across multiple devices), they’re reporting very similar power. Again, getting two power meters to record identically on a sprint is usually more luck than accuracy.

And finally, a 3rd sprint in this workout, roughly 1,000w, and this time Favero goes higher than Stages. So…yeah. Again, welcome to the world of trying to compare max powers on trainers. And this only gets messier the higher you go (e.g., 1,300w, 1,500w, etc.).

Finally, looking at the Mean-Max power curve for this workout, you can see it’s within 1.5% between the two units at 400w, and only slight separation as we go up to higher wattages.

Last up, we’ve got a Rouvy SIM ride from last night. This one was interesting, because I had some belt slip issues at one point. Stages has sent me simple instructions on how to tighten it (not hard, but not something I had time to do yet this morning). But you can see each time it slipped on a bit of a sprint, how things temporarily went sideways. Anyways, here’s the data. For the screenshot below, I excluded the last 10 minutes where the slippage occurs; I’ll show it later on below.

Here’s a bit of a surge I did to 700w, and no issues here:

Here are three lazy 800w sprints I did back-to-back. In this case, you can see slight differences with each one, but equally, all are essentially in the same ballpark. From either a racing or training standpoint, there’s no difference here. We’re again talking 1-second recording rates being the difference in these values.

Next, I tested high cadence on the unit, pedaling up to 190rpm before my legs decided it was enough. Had I tried it again, I’d probably gotten to 200rpm, which is the limit of the Stages SB200 from a cadence measurement standpoint. You can see the Favero’s flutter up to 198rpm here. I’m honestly not sure if that’s correct though, because you can also see down below it goes and oscillates a ton right as I easy-pedal, which doesn’t quite seem right either.

That said, the power between the two units for this high-cadence work was spot-on. Well done here.

Finally, as promised, here’s the moment the belt slipped on me, and then the immediate power offset. In confirming with Stages, the offset would exist until the belt stopped moving (which matches what I saw), because the bike immediately sees the belt slip and stops ‘trusting’ the values till it resets.

As noted above, Stages says I should only need to remove the casing and tighten a bolt one turn, and then I should be good to go. They don’t expect this to be a recurring issue once this is done. I’ll update this post once I’ve done that (it just happened last night) and then, longer-term, whether it pops back up again.

In any case, as for power meter accuracy, I’m not seeing anything that concerns me at any of the wattages I can ride. I simply can’t output 1,500w or other higher wattages, so I can’t replicate/test those (if you don’t know if you can hit those wattages, I promise you, you can’t). But at all the wattages I can test, the power is looking good accuracy-wise.

I’m looking forward to a bit more middle-ground on the ERG smoothing piece, which is something I’d thought I’d never say given how anti-smoothing it is. But the faster power update rate seen these days via WiFi especially, combined with the faster update rate of the SB200 itself (at 40x/second), means we are simply seeing far more human variability than we used to in the past.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Upcoming Accessories:

Just a super quick note that there are three upcoming near-term accessories for the Stage SB200 that I want to briefly mention. I don’t have any of these three accessories yet, but all three sound like they’re quite near-term (days/weeks to end of year at latest).

They are as follows:

Hydration Station (seen above): This is simply two extra water bottles off the front fork, kinda reminding me of the Peloton Bike setup. While they noted that many people might just have a table/etc. nearby, as with most accessories, there’s a market for potentially edge cases like this.

RigidRide: Don’t like all the movement (or the front-wheel-looking fork)? No problem, you can swap out the front faux-wheel and put a dual-pronged fork that you see below. This will reduce side-to-side movement and improve stability.

More Adjustable Seat Post: This seat post allows fore/after adjustability of the seat post assembly, rather than just the saddle adjustability of the stock unit. This is honestly one I feel probably should have been part of the base unit, given how common seat post adjustability is. There is not yet a photo available of this accessory.

Also of note is that there’s no pricing on any of these accessories at this point in time.

Wrap-Up:

I think the Stages SB200 is a very solid re-introduction into the marketplace for Stages. To begin with pricing, they managed to slice $400 off the previous 2020-era pricing, which is a very good start to things, especially given that the KICKR Bike Pro sits at $3,999 (though the KICKR BIKE SHIFT, which is probably a bit more comparable, sits at $1,999). Obviously, the dedicated smart bikes are more expensive than the recent trend of frames+trainers. But they also serve a slightly different, albeit partially overlapping market.

Looking at the previous SB20 unit, I think the SB200 is a massive upgrade over it, though. Starting off with the ‘form’ side of things, it’s just a much more consumer-friendly design, whether it be the weight/portability, or the styling/look, or aspects like the display and phone holders. I’m super happy with the vast majority of the hardware choices here. I also appreciate the inclusion of an app with a bunch of workouts built-in, and easy sync of other workouts into it (such as TrainingPeaks workouts). All for free, without a subscription.

The areas where I’m not as thrilled about would be the lack of seat movement fore/aft being included, the freehub sound when coasting, and some of the ERG mode smoothing pieces. Stages has promised a very near-term firmware update that will give users three options to sort the smoothing pieces out. So that should address that concern. The other two aren’t deal breakers for me though, so I don’t think most people need to overthink those too much.

Overall though, I’m keen to see where Stages takes this reincarnation, both on the tweaks/updates front, as well as potential future Stages SB200 accessories. And the same goes for firmware updates to the unit, giving the display more customization/control. All things fully within their capabilities via updates. And beyond that, I really appreciate Stages adopting the OpenBikeControl standard – hopefully that’s the start of a trend from more hardware players.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: Apple Watch Series 12 In-Depth Review: Worth Upgrading?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Apple Watch Series 12 arguably draws one of the biggest lines in the sand we’ve seen yet from Apple, within the core Apple Watch evolution. Not because it looks different from the outside (it doesn’t), or even because of the changed processor/chipset (moderately different). But instead, because of the changes in software features that Apple has tied to the new optical heart rate sensor package. As a result of that, there are a host of new features that are only available on the new Series 12 (and Ultra 4), which aren’t going back to previous Apple Watch Series owners.

Thus, for this review I’ll dive into all the nuances like I normally do – but I’m paying special attention to the new Readiness Score pieces, the heart rate accuracy of the much-touted new heart rate sensor, as well as ultimately whether or not this upgrade is worthwhile. And of course, within that, which people it makes the most sense for.

Note that as usual, there’s also the full video review above. There’s certainly some overlap, but also some pieces I cover within the video review that I don’t cover here, and vice versa.

With that – let’s get right into all the newness!

What’s New:

The Apple Watch Series 12 might look identical from the outside, but internally it’s got an entirely new processor, along with a boatload of new software features. Most of those features are lit up today from launch, but some of them won’t arrive until later on (a portion of the Audio Intelligence features). Further, all of the new Series 12 internals (processor-wise) are shared with the Apple Watch Ultra 4 that was launched the same day. Here’s how it differs from the Series 11:

Apple Watch Series 12 Hardware Updates/Changes:

– Gets new S11 chipset, which has features from the new A20 Pro chips of the iPhone 18 Pro
– Gets new secure audio processing exclave within that (for Audio Intelligence)
– Series 12 increased battery life to “over 2 days” (50 hours, technically)
– Series 12 adds revamped ‘Extended Battery’ (GPS) mode and new ‘Max Extended Mode’ (increasing workout GPS modes, though Apple doesn’t make battery claims on the Series 12)
– Boatloads of new bands for all of them, including new Nike bands
– New aluminum gold color
– New Hermes options as well

Apple Watch Heart Rate Sensing Hardware Update:

– New heart rate sensor with increased electrode surface area for better ECGs
– New photodiodes below it for better workout capture
– New LED array below that for better 24×7 HR readings
– New HR sensor is thinner (bump) than in the past
– Increased background (non-workout) HR readings to every 5 seconds (60x more than before)
– Increased HRV readings to every 5 minutes (24x more than before)
– Claim of Apple Watch Series 12/Ultra 4 “Most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable”
– Published their own white paper to support that claim, with competitor comparisons

New HRV Features:

– Added overnight HRV trending/recording within the Vitals app (as one of key metrics)
– Added new HRV into new ‘Daytime’ view in the Vitals app
– Requires 7 nights of initial data on a watch to get HRV trends in the Vitals app

New Readiness Score Feature:

– Each morning you’ll get a new score
– Score is based on a range of 0-10 (zero being worst, 10 being highest)
– Four core descriptors you can get: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, Go For It
– Can be viewed on the watch or the Fitness App
– Leverages your Sleep data, Vitals Metrics, Training Load, and recent Activity data
– Requires 7 nights of initial data for the HRV trends, before it can populate Readiness Scores

New Health App Redesign (on phone, coming later this year):

– Adds new AI summary and recommendations
– Adds Apple Intelligence guidance, including suggesting intervals
– Adds new Health Age: Based on Sleep, VO2Max, HRV, Heart Rate, Exercise Minutes, Steps, and optionally Labs
– Adds new longevity Tab, based on Nutrition, Metabolic, Overall Movement, Sleep, Hearing, Heart metrics, mental wellbeing
– Adds support for pulling in lab work
– Adds new VO2Max test (test can be done in living room in 6 minutes)
– Adds new other tests for flexibility, movement mechanics, strength, and more, which can be trended
– Health app coming later this year in beta in English

New Audio Intelligence features (on-device, some features later this year):

– Everything done on-device, without need for your phone (at least for immediate processing)
– [Available today] Adds Sound Recognition alerts for sirens, doorbells, baby crying, and more (shows up as text on watch)
– [Available today] Instant Shazam: Will instantly show you the name of songs when you raise your wrist
– [Available later 2026] Live Rewind: Double-tap the Digital Crown to get a text-only transcription of the last 15 seconds of spoken words
– [Available later 2026] Siri Recap: Will summarize conversations/spoken words heard around you into a recap that’s available on your phone.
– Can configure all features independently (enabled/disabled, plus further focus-mode-like controls for Siri Recap)

Got all that? Good, so let’s dive right into all the stuff you need to know when using the watch each day.

Daily Usage Basics:

In this section, I’m going to cover all the day-to-day basics of using the Apple Watch Series 12, mainly from the perspective of health, wellness, and sports/fitness. I’ll cover some of the other basics as well, but there’s plenty of other resources for things like playing back music, contactless payments, or 3rd party apps. None of which have changed in many years on the Apple Watch. So if you’re familiar with those from anytime in the last decade, it’s all the same as before. The key exception being the Audio Intelligence features, which I break out into their own section down below later in the review.

Of course, it’s worth noting that the Apple Watch Series 12 does indeed require an iPhone. It’s unable to be initially setup/configured without an iPhone, and you’ll need an iPhone 11 or newer that’s running iOS27 (the full list is here). Further, for the newer Audio Intelligence features, those need an iPhone capable of Apple Intelligence, which is essentially an iPhone 15 Pro, or any iPhone 16/17/18. That’s also true for the Apple Workout Buddy features too. Or really, anything depending on Apple Intelligence. But if you don’t care about those aspects, then just an iPhone 11 or newer will do fine.

With that set, on to the watch basics. The 2,000-nit display remains the same as last year, which is more than bright enough for even the sunniest of days. I live on a Mediterranean island, with plenty of bright, direct sun, and I’ve had zero issues seeing the display at any time. The screen size is the same as last year, which is almost identical to the Ultra 4. Both watches support minimum brightness down to 1-nit, which ensures it doesn’t blind you in the middle of the night. Here you can see the two screens side-by-side on a bright day in direct sun:

Next up, the interface basics. The Apple Watch Series 12 has essentially two buttons, though one of them also rotates and presses inwards. Plus, of course, the touchscreen itself. In the upper right, you’ve got the Digital Crown, which you can use to rotate through menus, and then also open the quick access menu to get to recently used apps (and Siri), like seen below.

Meanwhile, the lower right button opens up the controls dashboard to check battery, turn on the flashlight, set focus modes, and more. The focus modes will sync between your iPhone and watches instantly. Handy when you want to head to sleep early, simply toggle the bed icon on either watch or phone, and boom – all of your devices are instantly in sleep do-not-disturb mode.

Speaking of sleeping, it’s probably worth mentioning that one of my favorite new features of the Series 12 is the incredibly fast charging for topping off the battery. Just 5 minutes of charging is enough time to get 10 hours of sleeping time. This is achieved through both updated charging algorithms, as well as changes in the charging puck itself.
